m40: Cut each vegetable separately into 2 cm pieces. The sizes should be close so the cooking times agree.
Cook the aubergines alone 10 min over high heat in the oil: they drink the most and need the pan to themselves.
Set them aside, then cook the courgettes 8 min, the peppers 10 min and the onions 8 min, setting each aside.
Stew the diced tomatoes 10 min with the crushed garlic and the herbs.
Return all the vegetables to the tomato pan and simmer 20 min uncovered, stirring little so as not to crush them.
Taste and adjust. A ratatouille should be yielding but every vegetable still recognisable.
Make wells, crack in the eggs, cover and cook 6 min. White set, yolk running.
m41: Rinse the lentils and cook them 20 min in three times their volume of water, unsalted: salted too early, the skins toughen.
Salt at the end, drain and let them cool to warm. Warm lentils absorb dressing far better.
Make the dressing: mustard, vinegar, salt, then the oil in a stream, whisking to emulsify.
Chop the shallot very finely and leave it 5 min in the vinegar, which softens it.
Toss the warm lentils with the dressing and leave 15 min: this is when they take on the flavour.
Halve the cherry tomatoes and chop the parsley at the last moment.
Combine and adjust the seasoning, more firmly than seems necessary.
Crumble the feta over. Keeps four days and improves overnight.
m42: Rinse the bulgur and cover it with cold water, not boiling. Leave 20 min to swell: it cooks in the tomato juice and lemon.
Real tabbouleh is a parsley salad, not a grain salad: you need a lot, three bunches to a handful of bulgur.
Wash and dry the parsley thoroughly, pick the leaves and chop very finely with a knife, never in a processor which would bruise it.
Chop the mint the same way, in smaller quantity.
Dice the tomatoes very small and drain them 5 min in a sieve, keeping the juice.
Slice the spring onions, white and green alike.
Combine the drained bulgur, herbs, tomatoes and onions, then dress with lemon juice, oil and salt.
Chill 30 min and taste again: tabbouleh should be emphatically lemony.
m43: Slice the onions and peppers into strips rather than dice, so they stay visible in the dish.
Fry them 12 min over medium heat in a wide pan: they must collapse completely.
Add the cumin and paprika and stir 1 min off the heat, long enough to release their scent.
Pour in the chopped tomatoes, salt, and reduce 12 min uncovered.
The sauce is ready when it releases no more water and a spoon leaves a clean trail. That is the condition for the eggs to poach rather than boil.
Make four well-spaced wells and crack the eggs in gently.
Salt the yolks, cover and cook 6 min over low heat.
White set, yolk running. Serve straight from the pan with bread, without waiting.
m44: Dry the chicken thighs and brown them 8 min in the casserole, skin side down first. Set aside.
Sweat the sliced onions 8 min in the rendered fat over medium heat.
Add the ras el hanout and stir 1 min off the heat: the spices must warm without burning to release their aroma.
Return the chicken, add the carrots in lengths and 400 ml of hot stock.
Cover and simmer 40 min over low heat. The chicken should come away easily.
Add the dried apricots 15 min before the end; any earlier and they would dissolve.
Toast the almonds 4 min in a dry pan. Make the couscous, serve it separately and scatter the almonds at the last moment.
m45: Sweat the sliced onions 8 min in a little oil at the base of a large pot.
Add the ras el hanout and stir 1 min to wake it up.
Add the hard vegetables first, carrots and turnips, then the chopped tomatoes and water to come level.
Simmer 20 min covered, then add the courgettes in large lengths for 15 min more.
Fold in the drained chickpeas at the end, just long enough to heat through, 5 min.
Make the couscous: cover with one and a half times its volume of boiling salted water, cover 5 min, then separate the grains with a fork and a little oil.
Serve the couscous and vegetables separately, with the broth in a jug and harissa slackened with some of it on the side.
m46: Grate an onion rather than chopping it: the juice it releases keeps the meatballs moist.
Mix the lamb, grated onion, egg, breadcrumbs, cumin and parsley by hand. Do not overwork.
Rest 15 min in the fridge: the breadcrumbs absorb the moisture and the mixture holds better.
Shape 3 cm balls with damp hands, then brown them 6 min, rolling them around the pan.
Set them aside and sweat the second sliced onion 6 min in the same fat.
Add the chopped tomatoes, scrape the base and reduce 15 min.
Return the meatballs to the sauce and simmer 15 min covered, shaking the pan rather than stirring.
Add the coriander off the heat. Serve on couscous swollen with boiling water.
m47: Drain and rinse the chickpeas. Keep half for the hummus and half for the falafel.
For the hummus, blend the first half at length with the tahini, lemon juice, garlic and 4 spoonfuls of iced water. Blend at least 3 min: the duration is what makes it silky.
For the falafel, pulse the other half with the parsley, cumin and flour. The paste must stay grainy, not smooth.
Rest it 15 min in the fridge so it holds together, then shape tight balls between your palms.
Heat the oil to 170 °C: a crumb of paste should sizzle at once without browning within two seconds.
Fry the falafel 4 min in two batches, to a deep brown. Drain on a rack.
Serve straight away with the hummus, warm pitta and the diced raw vegetables.
m48: Slice the onions very finely and evenly; this is the key to the dish.
Fry them 20 min in the oil over medium heat, stirring often. They pass through blond and into brown: aim for a deep brown, just short of bitter.
Drain them on paper, where they will crisp as they cool. Keep the scented oil.
Cook the lentils 20 min in three times their volume of salted water.
Add the rinsed rice, the cumin, the cinnamon and two spoonfuls of the onion oil. Top up with water if needed.
Cover and cook 15 min on the lowest heat, then rest 10 min off the heat without lifting the lid.
Fluff with a fork, shape into a dome and cover with half the fried onions. Serve the rest and the yoghurt separately.
m49: Grate the onion and squeeze it in your hand to remove excess juice, which would make the mixture too wet.
Mix the meat, onion, chopped parsley and cumin, working it 2 min by hand: here you want it to turn sticky so it holds on the skewer.
Cover the bulgur with boiling salted water and leave 15 min to swell, then fluff with a fork.
Mould flat sausages around skewers, pressing firmly with a wet hand.
Cook 8 min in a very hot pan, turning a quarter turn every 2 min.
Make the sauce by mixing yoghurt, lemon juice, chopped mint and a pinch of salt.
Serve the skewers on the bulgur, sauce on the side.
m50: Cut the aubergines into 3 cm cubes, oil them generously and salt them.
Roast 30 min at 200 °C, turning halfway: they should be brown and yielding, not merely cooked.
Meanwhile tear the pitta into pieces and toast them 8 min in the oven until dry and brittle.
Warm the drained chickpeas 5 min in a pan with a little of their liquid and some cumin.
Make the sauce by whisking the yoghurt, tahini, crushed garlic and a little cold water to a coating texture.
Build on a serving dish: the toasted bread first, moistened with a spoonful of the chickpea liquid, just enough to soften it.
Then the warm chickpeas, the aubergines, and the sauce drizzled over.
Scatter with sesame and serve without delay, before the bread goes completely soft.
m51: Rinse the red lentils until the water runs clear: they foam far less afterwards.
Sweat the sliced onion 5 min, then add the grated garlic and ginger for 1 min.
Add the curry powder and warm it 1 min in the fat: dry spices only release their aroma on contact with fat.
Pour in the lentils, the tomatoes, the coconut milk and 300 ml water. Stir to lift the base.
Simmer 20 min over low heat, stirring regularly: lentils catch easily.
They are ready when they have collapsed completely and the dhal coats a spoon. Only now add salt.
Stir in the spinach off the heat; it cooks in the residual warmth. Serve with the rice.
m52: Drain and rinse the chickpeas, and take the frozen spinach out 10 min ahead.
Slice the onion and fry it 6 min over medium heat until translucent.
Add the grated garlic and the curry paste and fry it 2 min, stirring: it should darken and release its scent.
Cooking the paste in fat like this is what separates a built curry from one merely stirred together.
Pour in the coconut milk and bring to a bare simmer, never a rolling boil.
Add the chickpeas and the still-frozen spinach and simmer 15 min uncovered.
The sauce should thicken to a golden-green. Crush a few chickpeas to thicken it further.
Finish with lemon juice off the heat, which lifts everything. Serve with the rice.
m53: Mix the yoghurt, half the garam masala, and the grated ginger and onion. Marinate the cubed chicken in it at least 20 min.
Drain the pieces without wiping and sear 5 min over very high heat, in two batches. They should char without cooking through. Set aside.
Melt the remaining sliced onions 10 min in the same pan over medium heat.
Add the rest of the spices and warm 1 min: they should smell strong.
Pour in the chopped tomatoes, scrape the base, and reduce 20 min until the fat rises to the surface. That is the mark of a finished Indian sauce.
Return the chicken with its juices, add the cream, and simmer 10 min over low heat without boiling.
Taste: add a pinch of sugar if the tomatoes are sharp. Serve with the rice.
m54: Cut the potatoes into 2.5 cm cubes and the cauliflower into even small florets.
Heat the oil and throw in the whole cumin for 30 seconds, until it crackles and smells strong.
Add the sliced onion and brown it 8 min over medium heat.
Add the grated ginger and the turmeric and stir 1 min in the hot oil.
Add the potatoes, coat them in the spices and cook 10 min covered, stirring occasionally.
Add the cauliflower and continue 12 min covered, with no added water: the vegetables cook in their own steam.
Uncover for the last 5 min so the faces touching the pan brown a little.
Adjust the salt, add chopped coriander and serve with the rice.
m55: Slice the onions finely and fry them 15 min to a deep brown. Keep half back for serving.
Marinate the chopped vegetables in the yoghurt with the garam masala for 15 min.
Cook them 15 min over medium heat with half the fried onions, until tender but still holding.
Rinse the rice until the water runs clear, then boil it only 7 min in plenty of salted water: it must stay very firm.
Drain it and infuse the saffron in two spoonfuls of hot milk.
Layer in a casserole: vegetables, rice, saffron, fried onions. Repeat and finish with rice.
Seal tightly and cook 20 min on the lowest heat without ever lifting the lid. The trapped steam finishes the rice.
m56: Cut the fish into large 4 cm pieces and salt it 10 min ahead, which firms it.
Slice the onion and fry it 6 min over medium heat.
Add the turmeric and the crushed coriander seeds and stir 1 min in the oil.
Add the diced tomatoes and cook 8 min, until they break down completely.
Pour in the coconut milk and bring only to a simmer. A coconut curry must never boil or it splits.
Reduce 8 min uncovered to concentrate the sauce.
Slide the fish into the sauce without stirring and poach 8 min covered. Shake the pan if needed.
The fish is ready as soon as it flakes. Finish with lime off the heat and serve with the rice.
m57: Cut the chicken into 2 cm cubes and mix with the cornflour, a spoonful of soy and one of water. Leave 15 min.
This film of starch, called velveting, shields the meat from the wok's brutal heat and keeps it tender.
Cut everything in advance: pepper into squares, spring onions into lengths, ginger chopped. A stir-fry leaves no time to prepare.
Toast the cashews 4 min dry in the wok, then set aside.
Heat the wok until it just smokes, add the oil and sear the chicken 4 min without stirring for the first minute.
Push it aside, throw the ginger and pepper into the oil and stir-fry 2 min over high heat.
Combine, pouring the remaining soy down the scorching sides rather than onto the food: it caramelises instantly.
Cut the heat, add the cashews and spring onions and serve immediately on the rice.
m58: Cut the tofu into 2 cm cubes and poach them 2 min in simmering salted water. This firms them and stops them breaking up.
Drain them gently in a colander without stirring.
Heat a little oil and fry the chopped garlic and ginger 30 seconds without colouring.
Add the chilli paste and fry it 1 min: it should darken and scent the oil.
Pour in 200 ml water and the soy sauce and bring to a simmer.
Slide the tofu in and let it take on the sauce for 5 min without stirring. Push the pan rather than mix, so the cubes stay whole.
Slacken the cornflour in cold water and pour it in while shaking the pan. The sauce coats within 30 seconds. Spring onions to serve.
m59: The rice must be cold and dry, ideally cooked the day before. Hot rice would clump and go pasty.
Beat the eggs and cook them as a very thin omelette for 1 min in an oiled pan, then roll and slice into ribbons.
Heat the wok or pan empty until a drop of water vanishes instantly.
Stir-fry the diced ham 2 min over high heat, then add the peas for 2 min.
Add the rice and press it with the spatula to separate the grains. Stir-fry 4 min without stopping.
Pour the soy down the scorching sides of the wok rather than onto the rice: it caramelises instantly.
Fold in the omelette and spring onions off the heat, with a thread of sesame oil.
m60: Put the beef in the freezer for 15 min: it slices far more thinly when firm.
Cut it into very thin slices across the grain, which keeps it tender despite the flash cooking.
Marinate 10 min in half the soy and the cornflour.
Slice the onions into thick strips: too fine and they would disappear.
Heat the wok empty until a drop of water vanishes instantly, then add the oil.
Sear the beef 90 seconds in a single layer without stirring, then set it aside. It finishes in the residual heat.
Stir-fry the onions 5 min over high heat: they should colour at the edges and stay crisp in the middle.
Return the beef, add the rest of the soy and the sesame oil, toss 30 seconds and serve on the noodles.
m61: Poach the pork whole for 25 min in a litre of water with sliced ginger, at a bare simmer.
Skim carefully in the first minutes: a clear broth is half the dish.
Lift out the pork, let it rest 5 min and slice it thinly across the grain.
Strain the broth and season it with soy. Taste: it should be forthright, as the noodles will dilute it.
Shred the Chinese cabbage, keeping ribs and leaves separate.
Bring the broth to a simmer, drop in the ribs for 3 min then the leaves for 1 min.
Cook the noodles separately and divide between bowls: cooked in the broth they would cloud it.
Assemble noodles, cabbage and pork, pour over the boiling broth, finish with sesame oil and spring onions.
m62: Rinse the short-grain rice until the water runs clear, cook 15 min covered and rest 10 min without opening.
Dry the chicken breasts and score them lightly so they cook evenly.
Sear 6 min a side over medium heat in a barely oiled pan, starting with the thicker side.
Mix the soy, honey and mirin in a bowl.
Lower the heat, pour in the sauce and reduce 3 min, turning the chicken repeatedly to glaze it.
The sauce is ready when it coats the back of a spoon and bubbles thickly.
Rest the chicken 3 min before slicing, lay it on the rice and spoon the remaining glaze over. Sesame and spring onions.
m63: Heat 800 ml water with the sliced mushrooms and infuse 5 min below simmering point.
Never boil it: miso is alive, and high heat destroys its ferments and its scent.
Take a ladleful of hot broth into a bowl.
Slacken the miso into it with a fork until perfectly smooth, with no lumps.
Pour that mixture back into the pan off the heat, stirring gently.
Add the tofu in small cubes and let it warm through 2 min without stirring.
Cook the noodles separately and add them to the bowls.
Pour over the soup, scatter with shredded nori and spring onions, and serve at once.
m64: Flatten the pork to 1 cm and nick the fat around the edge, or the slice will curl in the pan.
Salt both sides and rest 10 min.
Set out three plates: flour, beaten egg, panko. Panko gives a lighter coating than fine breadcrumbs.
Coat, pressing firmly into the panko, then rest 10 min in the fridge.
Heat the oil to 170 °C. A crumb of panko should sizzle without browning instantly.
Fry 4 min a side to an even golden colour, then drain on a rack, never on paper.
Rest 3 min before slicing into 2 cm strips. Serve with very finely shredded cabbage and the rice.
m65: Cut the potatoes and carrots into 3 cm pieces and the onion into thick wedges.
Fry them 10 min in a little oil over medium heat, until the edges colour.
Cover with 700 ml stock and simmer 20 min, until the vegetables are tender.
Meanwhile make the roux: melt 30 g butter, add the flour and cook 3 min, stirring.
Add the curry powder off the heat and stir 1 min: this curry roux is what gives the dish its thick texture, quite unlike an Indian curry.
Slacken the roux with two ladles of hot stock to a smooth paste.
Stir it back into the pan and let it thicken 10 min over low heat.
Add the soy sauce, taste, and serve over short-grain rice.
m66: Open the coconut milk without shaking it and skim the thick cream from the top.
Heat that cream alone 5 min in a pan, until it splits and the oil beads on the surface.
Fry the curry paste in it 3 min, stirring: it should darken and release its scent. This step is the backbone of any Thai curry.
Add the chicken in pieces and coat it for 4 min.
Pour in the rest of the coconut milk and bring to a bare simmer, never a rolling boil: coconut milk splits.
Add the cubed aubergine and the green beans and simmer 15 min.
Season off the heat: fish sauce for salt, lime juice for acidity. Taste and adjust. Basil to serve.
m67: Soak the noodles 10 min in warm, not boiling, water: they finish in the wok and would otherwise turn pasty.
Mix the sauce separately: fish sauce, brown sugar and lime juice, stirred until the sugar dissolves.
Cut everything and line it up within reach. A pad thai takes five minutes.
Heat the wok very hot, sear the prawns 2 min and set aside.
Crack the eggs into the wok, let them set 20 seconds then scramble them roughly.
Add the drained noodles and the sauce and toss 3 min, lifting rather than stirring, until the noodles absorb all the liquid.
Cut the heat, return the prawns and add the bean sprouts, crushed peanuts and spring onions. Serve at once.
m68: Take the beef out 20 min ahead and dry it: cold, damp meat will not sear.
Sear 2 min a side in a scorching pan, for a brown crust and a pink centre.
Rest it 5 min on a board before slicing very thinly across the grain.
Make the dressing: fish sauce, lime juice, chopped chilli and a pinch of sugar.
Taste and adjust until sour, salty and hot are balanced, which is the whole point of the dish.
Slice the red onion very finely and rinse under cold water to soften its bite.
Combine the sliced beef, the cucumber in half-moons, the tomatoes, the onion and the dressing.
Add whole mint and coriander leaves at the last moment and serve at once: the salad weeps if it waits.
m69: Slice the pork thinly and marinate 15 min in the fish sauce, sugar and a little garlic.
Cook the noodles per the packet and rinse them at length under cold water to stop the cooking and wash off the starch.
Let them drain completely: wet noodles dilute the sauce at the bottom of the bowl.
Make the nuoc cham: dissolve the sugar in warm water, add fish sauce, lime juice, garlic and chilli.
Grate the carrot into fine batons and wash the herbs without chopping them; they are eaten whole.
Sear the pork 5 min over very high heat in a single layer, until the edges caramelise.
Build the bowls: salad and herbs at the bottom, then the noodles, then the pork still hot.
Scatter with crushed peanuts and pour the nuoc cham on as you eat, not before.
m70: Char the halved onion and sliced ginger in a dry pan, 5 min a side, until blackened in places. This is what gives the broth its depth.
Put them in a large pan with the chicken, the cinnamon, the five spice and 1.5 litres of cold water.
Bring gently to a simmer and skim carefully for 10 min. A broth that boils turns cloudy.
Let it barely tremble for 45 min uncovered, never above a gentle simmer.
Lift out the chicken, shred it, and strain the broth through a fine sieve.
Season the broth with fish sauce and taste: it should be forthright and salty, since the noodles will dilute it.
Cook the noodles separately and divide between bowls. Add the chicken, pour over the boiling broth, then the raw herbs and bean sprouts.
m71: Rinse the rice and cook it 15 min covered, then rest 10 min.
The method seasons each vegetable separately: that is what gives the bowl distinct flavours rather than one blurred taste.
Blanch the spinach 40 seconds, refresh, squeeze dry and season with garlic, sesame and salt.
Stir-fry the carrot batons 2 min with a pinch of salt and set aside.
Fry the sliced mushrooms 5 min over high heat with a little soy and set aside.
Sear the beef 4 min with the garlic and soy, until caramelised.
Put the rice in the bowls, arrange each topping in its own section and add a fried egg in the middle. Gochujang and sesame oil on the side, mixed in at the table.
m72: Use well-fermented, sour kimchi. Its acidity is what balances the fat of the pork.
Cut the belly into 5 mm slices and fry them 6 min over medium heat, with no added fat.
The pork renders its own fat, and everything else cooks in it.
Add the sliced onion and colour it 3 min over high heat.
Add the drained kimchi and stir-fry 4 min: cooking concentrates its flavour and softens its acidity.
Stir in the gochujang slackened with a spoonful of kimchi juice and cook 1 min.
Let it caramelise 2 min without stirring, so the base catches slightly.
Cut the heat, add the sesame oil and spring onions. Serve on the rice.
m73: Prick the sausages and blanch them 10 min in simmering water: this removes the excess salt and fat.
Drain, cut into thick rounds and brown them 6 min in a dry pan.
Set the sausages aside and melt the sliced onions 8 min in the rendered fat.
Add the grated ginger, the turmeric and the chilli and stir 1 min off the heat.
Pour in the chopped tomatoes and thyme, scrape the base, then return the sausages.
Simmer 30 min uncovered over low heat. The sauce should thicken and take on a deep orange colour.
Taste and adjust the chilli. Serve with plainly cooked rice, which balances it.
m74: Cut the chicken into large pieces and marinate 20 min in lime juice, crushed garlic and curry powder.
Caribbean colombo is milder and more aromatic than an Indian curry: it is not chasing heat.
Drain the chicken keeping the marinade, and brown it 8 min in a casserole on all sides.
Set aside, then sweat the sliced onions 8 min in the rendered fat.
Return the chicken and the marinade and add the vegetables in large pieces.
Add water only halfway up: the vegetables release a great deal as they cook.
Simmer 35 min covered, then uncover for 10 min to let the sauce reduce and coat.
Correct with lime before serving, with the rice.
m75: Dice the onions and peppers and fry them 8 min over medium heat in the oil.
Add the crushed garlic, then the cumin and paprika, and stir 1 min: the spices need to heat in fat to give their scent.
Pour in the chopped tomatoes and reduce 8 min uncovered, until the mixture darkens.
Add the drained and rinsed kidney beans and the sweetcorn.
Crush a ladle of beans against the side of the pan: that is what thickens a chilli with nothing added.
Simmer 25 min over low heat, stirring now and then and adding water if it catches.
Taste and adjust: a meatless chilli needs more salt and acidity than you would think.
Serve with the rice. Better the next day, once the spices have settled together.
m76: Slice the chicken into 1 cm strips across the width.
Toss it with the spices, a thread of oil and the juice of half a lime, and leave 15 min.
Cut the peppers and onion into strips the same size as the chicken, for even cooking.
Heat a cast-iron or large heavy pan until it just smokes.
Sear the chicken 5 min in a single layer, without stirring at first, so it marks.
Push it aside, add the vegetables and sear 5 min over high heat: they should stay crisp and char in places.
Warm the tortillas 30 seconds a side in a dry pan and keep them in a cloth.
Serve the pan scalding, with cream, lime and tortillas, everyone filling their own.
m77: Fry the sliced onion 6 min, then add the cumin and chilli and stir 1 min.
Add the drained black beans and 100 ml water, and crush them roughly with a fork.
Cook 8 min, stirring, to a thick purée that holds. Too loose and it would soak through the tortillas.
Warm the tortillas 20 seconds each so they turn supple and do not crack when rolled.
Fill each with a line of beans, roll tightly and lay them side by side, seam down, in a dish.
Coat with passata, covering the ends well, which would otherwise dry out.
Scatter grated cheese over the whole surface.
Bake 25 min at 190 °C until the sauce bubbles. Fresh coriander to serve.
m78: Cut the belly pork into large lardons and the sausages into thick lengths.
Brown them 8 min over medium heat in a casserole, with no added fat: the pork supplies what is needed.
Set the meats aside and sweat the sliced onions 8 min in that fat.
Add the crushed garlic and the bay and stir 1 min.
Return the meats, pour in the black beans with their liquid, which is thick and binds the dish, and 300 ml water.
Bring to a simmer and cook 40 min uncovered, stirring occasionally.
Crush a ladle of beans against the side to thicken it further.
Serve with the rice and orange wedges, whose acidity cuts the richness: the contrast is what makes the dish.
m79: Choose very fresh fish: it is not cooked in the usual sense, only denatured by acid.
Cut it into even 1.5 cm dice, removing every bone.
Squeeze the limes at the last moment; the juice loses its edge within minutes.
Salt the fish, cover it with juice and leave 15 min in the fridge. No longer: beyond that it turns dry and chalky.
Meanwhile slice the red onion very finely and rinse it in iced water.
Boil the sweet potato 20 min and cut it into thick rounds. Its sweetness balances the acidity.
Drain the fish partly, keeping some of the juice, which is called tiger's milk and is meant to be drunk.
Plate with the onion, chilli, coriander and sweetcorn, and serve immediately.
m80: Take the meat out 20 min ahead. Heat a casserole over high heat with no fat.
Spread the mince in it and let it colour 4 min untouched: that crust is where the flavour comes from.
Break it up with a spatula and continue 6 min, until all the water has evaporated.
Set the meat aside and sweat the diced onions and pepper 8 min in the rendered fat.
Add the cumin and chilli and stir 1 min off the heat.
Return the meat, pour in the tomatoes and the drained beans, and simmer 35 min over low heat.
Add the dark chocolate 5 min before the end: it brings no sweetness, only depth and colour.
Taste, adjust the salt and serve with the rice.
m81: Cook the pasta 3 min less than the packet says: it keeps swelling in the sauce and then in the oven.
Rinse it briefly under cold water to stop the cooking, then drain.
Make the béchamel: melt the butter, add the flour and cook 2 min without colour.
Pour in the hot milk in three additions, whisking hard each time, then cook 6 min until it coats a spoon.
Cut the heat and wait 1 min before adding the grated cheddar, in three lots. Too hot, the sauce makes the cheese string into lumps.
Season with nutmeg, pepper and salt, then fold through the pasta.
Tip into a buttered dish and cover with breadcrumbs mixed with a knob of melted butter.
Bake 20 min at 200 °C until golden and bubbling at the edges.
m82: Take the meat out 20 min ahead: cold, it cooks badly and shrinks.
Cut the potatoes into wedges, toss with the paprika, oil and salt, and roast 30 min at 200 °C.
Shape two patties without compacting the meat: the more you work it, the denser it gets. Press a shallow dip in the centre so they do not dome.
Salt the surface only, just before cooking. Salted too early, the meat weeps.
Heat a pan until it smokes and sear the patties 3 min untouched.
Turn them once only, lay the cheese on top and cover 2 min to melt it.
Toast the cut faces of the buns meanwhile: it forms a barrier that stops them going soggy.
Rest the patties 2 min before building the burger, or the juices escape into the bread.
m83: Cut the beef into 4 cm cubes and dry them thoroughly on kitchen paper.
Slice the onions and melt them 15 min over medium heat in a casserole: they should turn blond and sweet, the foundation of goulash.
Take the pot off the heat before adding the paprika, and stir 30 seconds. Paprika burns within seconds over high heat and turns bitter.
Add the meat and coat it, then the chopped tomatoes and water to come level.
Cover and simmer 1 h 15 on the lowest heat, stirring every 20 min.
Add the potatoes in large cubes and the peppers in strips, and continue 30 min uncovered.
The sauce thickens naturally on the potato starch: no flour needed.
Taste, adjust the salt and serve with a spoonful of cold cream dropped on top.
m84: Rinse the sauerkraut in cold water and squeeze it firmly: it is sold very salty and sharp.
Sweat the sliced onion 6 min in a casserole, then add the sauerkraut and fry it 5 min.
Moisten with the beer and add the bay. The beer brings the gentle bitterness that balances the cabbage's acidity.
Lay the belly pork on top, cover and cook 40 min over low heat.
Peel the potatoes and add them whole around the meat.
Add the sausages for the last 20 min only: any longer and they would split.
Check regularly that a little liquid remains, adding water if needed.
Serve the sauerkraut in the middle of the dish with the meats and potatoes around it, mustard on the side.
m85: Blitz the two meats briefly with the grated onion: beef and pork together give both flavour and tenderness.
Add the breadcrumbs and egg, mix by hand without overworking, then rest 15 min in the fridge.
Shape walnut-sized balls with damp hands, rolling them between your palms so they are truly round.
Brown them 8 min in butter over medium heat, shaking the pan regularly rather than turning them one by one. Set aside.
Boil the potatoes 20 min in salted water and mash with butter and a little hot milk.
In the meatball pan, make a roux with the flour and the rendered fat, 2 min.
Whisk in the cream and 200 ml water, let it thicken 5 min, then return the meatballs for 10 min.
Serve with the mash and a spoonful of jam alongside: the sweet-sour note is inseparable from the dish.
m86: Peel the potatoes and start them in cold salted water, 25 min.
Sweat the finely diced onions and carrots 8 min over medium heat.
Add the mince, raise the heat and spread it out untouched for 3 min so it colours, then break it up.
Cook 8 min more: all the water must evaporate and the meat begin to fry, or the pie will be watery.
Add the tomato purée and rosemary, stir 2 min, then 200 ml water and reduce 12 min.
Add the peas at the end, straight from frozen.
Mash the potatoes with butter and hot milk, to a firm mash rather than a loose one.
Spread over the meat and rake with a fork: the ridges brown and give the texture. Bake 25 min at 200 °C.
m87: Poach the fish 6 min in barely simmering milk, never boiling. Lift it out as soon as it flakes and keep the milk.
Boil the potatoes 20 min in salted water.
Make the béchamel with the poaching milk: butter and flour roux for 2 min, then the milk in three additions, whisking.
Cook 6 min until it coats, then add the chopped dill and the peas straight from frozen.
Flake the fish into the sauce in large pieces and fold gently so it does not turn to paste.
Tip into a dish and let it cool for 10 min: a scalding filling would make the mash slide off.
Mash the potatoes with butter, spread over the fish and rake with a fork.
Scatter with gruyère and bake 25 min at 190 °C, until the sauce bubbles at the edges.
m88: Dry the chicken thighs and brown them 8 min in a casserole, skin down first. Set aside.
Sweat the sliced onions 8 min in the rendered fat over medium heat.
Slacken the peanut butter in 200 ml hot water, whisking to a smooth cream with no lumps.
Add the chopped tomatoes to the onions and reduce 8 min.
Pour in the slackened peanut paste, stirring constantly: added at once and left alone, it catches immediately.
Return the chicken, add the sweet potato and carrots in large pieces, and water halfway up.
Simmer 40 min covered, stirring every 10 min. Groundnut catches on the base very easily.
The sauce is ready when the peanut oil rises to the surface. Serve with the rice.
m89: Yassa rests entirely on the marinade: do not cut it short, it is what makes the dish.
Slice the onions into strips; they should weigh almost as much as the chicken.
Mix the juice of three lemons, the mustard, the oil, the chilli and the onions, and submerge the chicken.
Marinate at least 2 h, ideally overnight, turning once.
Drain the chicken keeping the marinade and brown it 10 min over high heat in a casserole.
Set it aside, then tip in the drained onions and stew them 20 min over medium heat, until they collapse completely.
Add the marinade liquid and the bay, return the chicken and simmer 25 min covered.
Uncover for 10 min to reduce. The sauce should be glossy and emphatically lemony. Serve with the rice.
m90: Brown the sliced chorizo 4 min over medium heat in a pan, with no added fat.
It releases a red, scented fat: that is what carries the whole dish, so do not throw it away.
Lift out the rounds and sweat the sliced onion 6 min in that fat.
Add the crushed garlic and the paprika off the heat and stir 30 seconds to avoid bitterness.
Add the drained and rinsed white beans with 100 ml water and fold gently.
Crush a ladle of beans against the side of the pan: that is what thickens the sauce with no cream or flour.
Simmer 10 min over low heat, shaking the pan rather than stirring, so they do not break up.
Return the chorizo, add chopped parsley and a thread of raw oil. Serve warm with bread.
d01: Choose apples that break down, like Golden or Reinette: an eating apple would stay in pieces.
Peel, core and cut them into quarters of even thickness so they cook at the same rate.
Put them in a heavy pan with only 50 ml water. Apples already hold a great deal.
Add the sugar and cinnamon, cover and cook 15 min over low heat, stirring twice.
They are ready when they collapse under the spoon without resistance.
Crush with a fork to keep some texture, or blend for a smooth purée: it is a matter of taste.
Add the lemon juice off the heat: added hot it evaporates, added cold it lifts the fruit.
Jar it while still hot and seal. Keeps five days in the fridge.
d02: Blanch the rice 2 min in boiling water and drain. This removes the surface starch that would make it stick.
Split the vanilla pod, scrape the seeds into the cold milk and add the pod too.
Bring the milk to a simmer, then add the rice.
Cook 30 min over very low heat, stirring every 5 min with a wooden spoon so the base does not catch.
The rice should stay coated in milk: if it dries out, add a little hot milk.
Add the sugar only at the end. Added early, it stops the rice swelling properly.
Continue 5 min, then remove the pod.
Pour into ramekins and leave to cool. It thickens further as it cools, so do not chase thickness while hot.
d03: Squeeze the citrus at the last moment: the juice loses its scent within minutes in the air.
Peel the oranges to the flesh with a knife, removing all the bitter white pith.
Cut every fruit to a similar size, so none dominates the spoonful.
Add the bananas last and dress them immediately with lime juice, or they blacken within ten minutes.
Dissolve the honey in a spoonful of warm juice rather than pouring it in as it is.
Pour over the fruit and fold gently, without crushing.
Chill 30 min: that rest draws out the juices and pulls the flavours together.
Shred the mint at the very last moment before serving, or it darkens.
d04: Take the yoghurt out 10 min ahead: ice cold, it masks its own flavour.
Chop the walnuts roughly with a knife rather than a processor, to keep uneven pieces.
Toast them 3 min in a dry pan over medium heat, stirring constantly.
They are ready the moment they smell fragrant; a few seconds more and they turn bitter.
Cool them on a cold plate: left in the hot pan they would keep cooking.
Spoon the yoghurt into bowls and smooth it with the back of a spoon.
Drizzle the honey over without stirring, to keep the layers distinct.
Scatter the walnuts at the very last moment, or they soften.
d05: Separate the eggs cold, as they separate more cleanly, but let the whites come to room temperature before whisking.
Break the chocolate into pieces and melt it over a bain-marie, over low heat, never letting the water boil.
Any water or steam falling in would seize the chocolate and make the mousse grainy.
Off the heat, beat in the yolks one at a time: the mixture thickens and turns glossy.
Whisk the whites with a pinch of salt, adding the sugar in three lots once they start to foam.
They should hold a soft peak, not a brittle one: over-whisked, they refuse to fold in.
Slacken the chocolate first with a third of the whites, beating firmly, then fold in the rest with a spatula, lifting from the bottom.
Spoon into glasses and chill at least 4 h. A rushed mousse never sets properly.
d06: Take the fromage blanc out 15 min ahead and whisk it 30 seconds to smooth it.
Set aside a handful of whole raspberries for serving.
Blend the rest with the sugar and a squeeze of lemon to a smooth coulis.
Pass through a fine sieve, pressing with a ladle: raspberry seeds spoil the texture.
Taste and adjust the sugar to the fruit's acidity, which varies enormously from punnet to punnet.
Divide the fromage blanc between glasses and smooth the surface.
Pour the coulis over at the last moment: added early, it blends in and gives a dull pink.
Sit the whole raspberries on top and serve well chilled.
d07: Choose bananas that are ripe but still firm: over-ripe, they collapse in the oven.
Split them lengthways without separating the halves and lay them in a dish.
Dot butter into the cut, then pour over the honey and rum.
Squeeze the lime over: its acidity is what stops the dish being cloying.
Bake 15 min, basting once with the juices in the dish.
They are ready when the flesh turns pearly and the juice has caramelised at the edges.
Serve scalding, perhaps with a spoonful of cold fromage blanc for contrast.
d08: Bring the milk to a simmer with both sugars, stirring to dissolve.
Watch it: milk rises and boils over in seconds.
Rain the semolina in with one hand while whisking with the other, without stopping.
Tipped in at once, it forms lumps that cannot be rescued.
Cook 8 min over low heat, stirring constantly: semolina thickens abruptly near the end.
Add the raisins, previously plumped 10 min in warm water.
Pour into ramekins at once and smooth the tops, before it sets in the pan.
Cool 2 h. Cover with cling film touching the surface if you want to avoid the skin that forms.
d09: Choose apples that hold their shape, like Bramley or Canada.
Core them without piercing the base, or the filling escapes and burns on the tray.
Score the skin all the way round at mid-height: it would otherwise split under the steam pressure.
Plump the raisins 10 min in a little hot water, then drain.
Fill each cavity with butter, brown sugar, cinnamon and raisins, pressing down.
Sit them in a dish with two spoonfuls of water in the base, so the escaping sugar does not burn.
Bake 30 min at 180 °C, basting with the juices halfway.
They are ready when a knife tip enters without resistance. Serve warm with the caramelised juices.
d10: The butter must come straight from the fridge: cold it forms crumbs; soft it would give a sticky paste.
Cut it into small dice and add the flour, sugar and oats.
Rub between your fingertips until you have uneven crumbs.
Do not aim for uniformity: it is the unevenness that gives the crunch.
Dice the apples to 2 cm and spread them in a dish without packing them down.
Cover generously with the crumble, without pressing: the topping must stay loose to crisp.
Bake 25 min at 190 °C, until golden and the apple juices bubble at the edges.
Rest 10 min: straight from the oven a crumble is scalding and still soft.
d11: Use stale bread, ideally a day old: fresh bread soaks through and tears.
Beat the eggs, milk and sugars until the sugar has dissolved.
Pour into a shallow dish rather than a bowl, so the slices can lie flat.
Soak each slice 30 seconds a side, no more: over-soaked, it falls apart in the pan.
Heat the butter over medium heat and wait for it to foam without browning.
Cook 3 min a side without moving the slices, to an even caramel colour.
Do not crowd the pan: the slices must brown, not steam against one another.
Serve immediately, dusted with sugar. French toast does not wait.
d12: Choose firm pears, barely ripe: ripe ones will disintegrate in the syrup.
Peel them keeping the stalk, which lets you handle them without damage.
Rub them with lemon at once so they do not brown while you make the syrup.
Bring the wine, sugar, cinnamon and orange zest to a simmer, stirring to dissolve the sugar.
Lay the pears in and cover with a disc of baking paper: any part above the liquid would colour unevenly.
Poach 25 min at a gentle simmer, turning them halfway.
Lift them out and reduce the syrup by half, 10 min over high heat, until it coats a spoon.
Pour over the pears and let them cool in it. Far better the next day, once the colour has penetrated.
d13: Take the eggs and yoghurt out 30 min ahead: cold ingredients stop the batter emulsifying.
Empty the yoghurt pot into a bowl and keep the pot; it is the measure for everything else.
Whisk the yoghurt, sugar and eggs 2 min, until the mixture pales and nearly doubles.
Add the sifted flour and baking powder and mix only enough to lose the lumps.
Overworked, the batter develops gluten and the cake turns rubbery.
Fold in the oil in a stream, then the lemon zest, in three movements.
Pour into a buttered floured tin and bake 30 min at 180 °C without opening the door before 25 min.
A knife blade in the centre should come out dry. Turn out while still warm.
d14: Soak the gelatine leaves 10 min in a large bowl of very cold water, kept apart from one another.
Split the vanilla pod and scrape the seeds into the cream, adding the pod too.
Heat the cream and sugar over low heat to 80 °C, when small bubbles form at the edges.
Never boil it: boiled cream tastes of cooked milk and turns chalky.
Squeeze the gelatine out between your hands and stir it in off the heat, whisking until fully dissolved.
Remove the pod, then pour into glasses through a fine sieve.
Let it cool to room temperature before refrigerating: thermal shock costs a panna cotta its silkiness.
Chill 4 h. It should wobble slightly when you shake the glass, or it has set too firm.
d15: Heat the oven to 180 °C and line the tin with baking paper, leaving an overhang so you can lift it out.
Melt the chocolate and butter over a bain-marie, stirring to a smooth glossy mixture.
Let it cool 5 min: poured scalding onto the eggs, it would cook them.
Whisk the sugar and eggs 2 min until pale, without trying to aerate them.
Fold in the warm chocolate, then the sifted flour in three additions, with a spatula.
Add the chopped walnuts and pour into the tin, levelling it roughly.
Bake exactly 22 min. The brownie must come out wobbling at the centre: the underbaking is what makes it fudgy.
Cool completely in the tin before cutting, or it collapses.
d16: Take the butter out 1 h ahead: it should be soft, neither melted nor hard.
Cream it with the brown sugar for 3 min, until pale and airy.
Add the egg and beat another minute so it fully incorporates.
Add the flour and baking powder and mix as little as possible, just until the flour disappears.
Fold in the chocolate in rough chunks rather than chips: the pockets of melted chocolate are the whole point.
Chill the dough 30 min. This step stops the cookies spreading into thin discs.
Shape balls spaced 5 cm apart on the tray, without flattening them.
Bake 11 min at 180 °C: they should come out still soft in the middle and firm up on the tray.
d17: Whisk the eggs and sugar 3 min, until the mixture falls from the whisk in a ribbon.
Add the sifted flour and baking powder, then the finely grated lemon zest.
Melt the butter and let it cool before folding it in: scalding, it would cook the eggs.
Chill the batter at least 30 min, ideally 2 h. The shock between cold batter and hot oven creates the hump.
Butter and flour the moulds even if they are non-stick; the batter grips easily.
Fill them only three quarters full, with a piping bag or two spoons.
Bake 9 min at 200 °C, without opening the door for the first 6 minutes.
Turn them out the moment they leave the oven: left in the tin they soften.
d18: Freeze the sliced bananas the day before: that is what gives the thick texture, without ice.
Take the raspberries out 5 min ahead so the blender does not labour.
Put the frozen fruit in the bowl with the yoghurt, but no liquid at the start.
Blend in pulses, scraping the sides, to the texture of thick soft-serve.
Add liquid only drop by drop if the blender stalls: too much and the bowl becomes a drink.
Pour into a cold bowl, straight from the fridge, which slows the melting.
Smooth the surface with the back of a spoon in waves.
Arrange the oats, honey and whole fruit in bands, and serve immediately.
d19: Butter a dish generously and spread the cherries in a single layer, without stoning them if you follow tradition.
The stones lend an almond note to the batter during baking; warn your guests.
Whisk the eggs and sugar 2 min until the mixture pales.
Add the sifted flour all at once and whisk hard until the lumps disappear.
Loosen with the milk poured in a stream, whisking constantly: the batter should be as loose as pancake batter.
Rest 15 min, which lets the flour hydrate and gives a finer texture.
Pour gently over the cherries without shifting them.
Bake 35 min at 180 °C. A clafoutis puffs then sinks as it cools, which is normal.
d20: Use a straight, fairly wide mug: in a narrow one the batter overflows or stays raw at the centre.
Mix all the dry ingredients with a fork first, directly in the mug.
Scrape the corners of the base well, where flour gathers and forms dry pockets.
Add the milk and oil and beat with a fork for 30 seconds, to a perfectly smooth batter.
Do not fill the mug beyond halfway: the batter doubles as it cooks.
The cake should be risen and still slightly damp on top: ten seconds more and it turns rubbery.
Let it settle 1 min before eating; it is scalding at the centre.
d21: Choose firm, sharp apples like Reinette: a floury one would turn to purée.
Peel them, cut into thick quarters and rub with lemon.
Make a dry caramel: rain the sugar into a heavy tin over medium heat, never stirring with a spoon.
Tilt the tin to spread it. The caramel is ready at an amber colour, just before it smokes.
Take it off the heat and beat in the diced butter, which makes the caramel foam violently.
Pack the quarters upright and very tight, rounded side down, then cook 20 min over low heat.
Lay the pastry over, tucking the edges down inside the tin, and bake 30 min at 190 °C.
Wait 10 min before turning out: too soon and the caramel runs, too late and it welds itself in.
d22: Heat the oven to 180 °C, butter a 22 cm tin and line it with baking paper.
Melt the chocolate and butter over a bain-marie, stirring to a smooth glossy mixture.
Let it cool 5 min before going on: this is the mistake that makes the batter grainy.
Whisk the eggs and sugar 3 min, until doubled in volume and falling in a ribbon.
Fold in the warm chocolate in three additions with a spatula, lifting rather than stirring.
Sift the flour over and fold in the minimum necessary.
Bake 22 min. It should be set 2 cm in from the edge and still wobbling at the centre.
Cool completely in the tin. Much better the next day, taken out 30 min before serving.
d23: Blind bake the pastry case: prick it, cover with paper and weights, 20 min at 180 °C.
Remove the weights and give it 5 min more to dry the base, or the curd will make it soggy.
Zest two lemons before juicing them: you cannot zest a squeezed lemon.
Whisk the yolks, sugar, cornflour and lemon juice together cold, in a pan.
Heat over medium heat, whisking constantly, until it thickens, about 5 min. It must bubble 30 seconds to cook the cornflour.
Off the heat, beat in the cold diced butter: it gives the shine and the set.
Fill the case and smooth it, then whisk the whites to a firm meringue with the remaining sugar added in three lots.
Pipe it on in peaks and colour 8 min at 200 °C, or with a blowtorch.
d24: Blitz the biscuits to a fine powder and mix with the melted butter, to the texture of wet sand.
Press firmly into the base of a springform tin with the back of a spoon, taking it slightly up the sides.
Chill 20 min while you make the filling: a cold base will not merge into the cream.
Beat the cheeses, sugar and zest 2 min on low speed. Over-beaten, the mixture takes in air and cracks in the oven.
Add the eggs one at a time, mixing as little as possible between each.
Pour onto the base and bake 50 min at 150 °C. A low temperature is the key to a cheesecake without cracks.
Turn the oven off and let it cool inside with the door ajar for 1 h: slow cooling prevents sinking.
Chill overnight. A cheesecake cut the same day does not have the right texture.
d25: Separate the eggs and take the mascarpone out 20 min ahead: cold, it lumps beyond rescue.
Whisk the yolks and sugar 4 min, until pale and falling in a ribbon.
Add the mascarpone in three additions, whisking slowly so it does not split.
Whisk the whites to soft peaks with a pinch of salt, then fold them in with a spatula.
Make a strong coffee and let it cool: hot, it would soak the biscuits instantly.
Dip each biscuit for one second a side, no more. They must stay firm at the core.
Alternate biscuits and cream in two layers, finishing with smoothed cream.
Chill at least 6 h. Dust with sieved cocoa just before serving, never in advance.
d26: Soak the dried apricots 20 min in warm rum, which plumps and flavours them.
Whisk the flour, eggs and sugar to a thick smooth paste with no lumps.
Loosen with the milk poured in a stream, whisking constantly: added at once it makes lumps you cannot rescue.
Add the soaking rum and rest the batter 30 min at room temperature.
That rest hydrates the flour and gives a far its dense, smooth texture, quite unlike a custard tart.
Butter a dish generously and spread the drained fruit in it.
Pour the batter over and bake 45 min at 190 °C: a far rises a lot then sinks, which is normal.
Cool completely. It is eaten warm or cold, never scalding.
d27: Line the tin with the pastry, prick the base with a fork and return it to the fridge for 15 min.
Scatter the ground almonds over the whole base: they absorb the apple juices and protect the pastry.
Peel the apples, halve them, core them and slice into 3 mm lamellae.
Arrange them in an overlapping rosette from the edge inwards. Packed tight, they do not collapse in the oven.
Dust with sugar and cinnamon, then dot butter over the whole surface.
Bake 45 min at 180 °C, placing the tart low in the oven so the base cooks from below.
It is ready when the tips of the slices have browned and the base is golden.
Cool on a rack rather than in the tin, or the steam softens the pastry.
d28: Heat the milk with the split and scraped vanilla pod, and infuse 10 min off the heat.
Whisk the eggs, sugar and cornflour cold, to a perfectly smooth mixture.
Pour the hot milk onto the eggs in a stream while whisking, rather than the reverse, which would cook them.
Return everything to the pan and cook over medium heat, whisking without stopping.
It thickens suddenly around 82 °C. Continue 2 min to cook out the cornflour, or the tart tastes floury.
Pour boiling onto the pastry base, which starts cooking it immediately and stops it going soggy.
Bake 40 min at 180 °C, until the surface is blotched dark brown in places.
Cool completely then chill 4 h before cutting. A warm flan will not slice cleanly.
d29: Take the berries out of the freezer if frozen, but do not thaw them: they would release too much water.
Dice the apples to 2 cm and mix them with the berries in a dish.
Do not sugar the fruit: the crumble has enough, and sugar would draw out yet more juice.
Rub the flour, cold diced butter, brown sugar and ground almonds between your fingertips.
Stop as soon as you have crumbs of uneven size, without chasing uniformity.
Cover the fruit with a thick layer, without pressing: a packed crumble bakes like a biscuit.
Bake 40 min at 180 °C. Berries release a lot of juice: it should bubble at the edges.
Rest 15 min before serving, to let the juice thicken.
d30: Take the filo out at the last moment and keep it under a damp cloth: it dries and cracks within minutes.
Roughly chop the almonds and walnuts and mix them with the sugar and cinnamon.
Melt the butter and let it settle: use only the clear part, as the milk solids would burn.
Butter the tin, then layer six sheets, brushing each one lightly.
Spread a third of the nuts, cover with three buttered sheets, and repeat twice.
Finish with six sheets and score into diamonds right through to the base with a sharp knife.
Cutting before baking is essential: afterwards the pastry shatters under the blade.
Bake 45 min at 170 °C, then pour the cold honey-lemon syrup over the scalding baklava. Leave overnight to soak.
d31: Make the sweet pastry: rub the flour and cold butter together, add the sugar, an egg and a pinch of salt.
Bring it together without kneading, flatten into a disc, wrap and chill 30 min. Kneaded pastry turns hard.
Make the pastry cream: whisk yolks, sugar and cornflour, pour on the hot milk, then cook 3 min whisking.
Add the rum off the heat, cover with cling film touching the surface and cool completely. Warm cream would soak the pastry.
Roll out two thirds of the pastry and line the tin, taking it well up the sides.
Fill with the cold cream leaving a 1 cm margin, then cover with the remaining rolled pastry and seal the edges.
Brush with beaten egg and score the top with a fork, the traditional crosshatch.
Bake 45 min at 180 °C. Cool completely: warm, a gâteau basque has not yet found its texture.
d32: Wash and hull the strawberries, keeping the best ones for decoration.
Blend half the strawberries with half the sugar, then sieve to remove the seeds.
Soak the gelatine 10 min in very cold water, then dissolve it in 3 spoonfuls of warmed coulis.
Warm it, do not heat it: above 60 °C gelatine loses its setting power.
Whip the very cold cream to soft peaks with the remaining sugar. Over-whipped, it turns grainy.
Fold the set coulis into the cream in three additions with a spatula.
Line the mould with biscuits soaked in a lemony strawberry syrup, then alternate mousse and sliced strawberries.
Chill at least 6 h. Turn out by passing a warm cloth around the mould.
d33: Make the batter the day before: this is a requirement, not a convenience. The rest drives out the air bubbles.
Heat the milk with the split vanilla, without boiling, and infuse 10 min.
Whisk the eggs and sugar, then add the sifted flour all at once and whisk to a smooth batter.
Pour in the warm milk in a stream, then the melted butter and the rum, whisking without incorporating air.
Sieve it, cover and chill 24 h. The batter should be as fluid as pancake batter.
Butter the moulds very generously and fill them three quarters full with the cold batter, well stirred.
Bake 15 min at 230 °C to form the crust, then drop to 180 °C and continue 45 min.
Turn them out the instant they leave the oven: cooled in the moulds, cannelés soften and lose their crust.
d34: Take the butter and eggs out 1 h ahead: a cold mixture will not emulsify and the marbling will fail.
Cream the soft butter and the sugar 4 min, until pale and fluffy.
Add the eggs one at a time, beating well between each so the emulsion holds.
Fold in the sifted flour and baking powder in three additions, mixing the minimum necessary.
Divide the batter into two equal parts and add the sifted cocoa and the milk to one.
The milk is essential: cocoa absorbs moisture, and that half would otherwise be drier than the other.
Spoon alternately into a loaf tin, two spoonfuls at a time, then draw a knife through once in a zigzag.
Bake 45 min at 170 °C. Marbling too much would give a uniformly brown cake, with no pattern.
n01: Start the rice first: 12 min in boiling salted water, then 5 min resting off the heat, covered.
Cut the chicken into even 1.5 cm strips and the courgettes into 5 mm half-moons.
Dry the chicken and salt it. Heat a pan until a drop of water vanishes instantly.
Sear the chicken 6 min over high heat, in a single layer and without stirring for the first minute so it colours. Set aside.
In the same pan, stir-fry the courgettes 6 min over high heat with the crushed garlic and thyme.
They should brown in places and stay firm: stirred too much or cooked too gently, they weep and collapse.
Return the chicken, zest the lemon straight into the pan then squeeze in the juice, and stir 1 min off the heat.
The zest brings the scent, the juice the acidity: you need both. Serve on the rice.
n02: Rinse the short-grain rice until the water runs clear, cook 15 min covered and rest 10 min without opening.
Cut the cucumber and carrot into fine batons, salt them lightly and dress with rice vinegar. Leave them to pickle while you do the rest.
Dry the salmon fillets and salt them 10 min ahead, which firms the flesh.
Mix the soy and honey in a bowl, so you are not measuring mid-cook.
Heat a pan over medium-high heat and sear the salmon 4 min skin side down, untouched: the skin must turn crisp.
Turn it for 2 min only, then lower the heat.
Pour in the sauce and let it glaze 2 min, spooning it over the fish, until it turns syrupy.
Plate on the rice with the drained pickled vegetables, and scatter with sesame.
n03: Put a large pan of salted water on and start the pasta: everything else happens while it cooks.
Wash the spinach and spin it thoroughly dry: any remaining water would thin the sauce.
Soften the sliced garlic 1 min in a little fat over low heat, without colouring it.
Add the spinach in handfuls and wilt it 3 min: it reduces by three quarters.
Pour in the cream and the lemon zest and simmer 2 min so it thickens slightly.
Drain the pasta a minute early, keeping a large ladle of the cooking water.
Tip it into the pan with some of that water and the parmesan, and toss hard for 1 min: the starch binds sauce to pasta.
Squeeze the lemon juice in off the heat only, or the cream may split.
n04: Put the beef in the freezer for 15 min, which lets you slice it very thinly across the grain.
Mix it with the cornflour and half the soy and leave 10 min: this coating shields the meat from the fierce heat.
Cut the broccoli into small florets and slice the stalks, then blanch 3 min and refresh under cold water.
This head start guarantees they cook through without the stir-fry dragging on.
Heat the wok empty until it smokes, add the oil and sear the beef 2 min without stirring at first. Set aside.
Stir-fry the chopped garlic and ginger 20 seconds, then the broccoli 2 min.
Return the beef and pour the remaining soy down the scorching sides of the wok rather than onto the food.
Add the cooked noodles and the sesame oil, toss 1 min and serve at once.
n05: Heat the oven to 210 °C. A properly hot oven from the start is what separates roasting from stewing.
Cut the sweet potato into 3 cm cubes and the red onion into thick wedges.
Toss them in a bowl with the oil, paprika and salt, until every piece is coated.
Spread them on a tray in a single layer, not touching. Crowded, they would steam.
Dry the chicken thighs, salt them and sit them on the vegetables, skin up.
Roast 30 min without opening the oven. Opening it drops the temperature and lengthens the cooking.
Check by piercing a thigh: the juice should run clear.
Rest 5 min and serve with the yoghurt let down with lemon juice and a pinch of salt.
n06: Start the rice, 12 min; it will be ready with the curry.
Dry the prawns on kitchen paper: wet, they drop the pan's temperature.
Skim two spoonfuls of the thick part of the coconut milk and heat them alone 3 min, until the oil beads.
Fry the curry paste in it 2 min, stirring: it should darken and smell strong. This is the step that builds the flavour.
Add the sliced pepper and the rest of the coconut milk, then simmer 6 min without ever boiling.
Slide the prawns into the sauce and count exactly 3 min: beyond that they turn rubbery.
Cut the heat, squeeze in the lime and add the chopped coriander.
Taste and adjust: a Thai curry is always balanced at the end, never at the start.
n07: Clean the mushrooms dry with a cloth rather than under water, which they soak up like a sponge.
Slice them fairly thick, 5 mm, so they do not vanish in the cooking.
Heat a pan over high heat, add the mushrooms and leave them alone for 2 min: they must sear before they weep.
Stir and continue 4 min, then salt only now, at the end.
Add the chopped shallot for 2 min, then the cream, and simmer 3 min to thicken.
In a second pan, brown the gnocchi 6 min straight from the pack, without boiling them: that is what gives them a crust.
Combine with the cream off the heat and fold gently.
Parmesan and parsley at the last moment, with a generous turn of pepper.
n08: Cook the rice 12 min and, the moment it is drained, dress it with lemon and salt: it absorbs best while warm.
Drain and rinse the black beans, then warm them 5 min in a pan with the cumin and a little oil.
Crush them lightly with a fork against the base of the pan, which makes them creamy and easier to eat from a bowl.
Dice the tomatoes and drain them 5 min in a sieve: their juice would flood the bowl.
Cut the avocado at the last moment and dress it immediately with lime so it does not brown.
Chop the coriander roughly, stalks included, which have as much flavour as the leaves.
Put the rice in the bottom of the bowl and arrange each element in its own section rather than mixed.
Serve with an extra lime wedge: the acidity is adjusted at the table.
n09: Rinse the rice and cook it 15 min covered, then rest without opening.
Flatten the chicken breasts between two sheets of baking paper to an even 1.5 cm.
Salt the flour rather than the meat, then coat: flour, beaten egg, panko pressed on firmly.
Rest 10 min in the fridge: the coating adheres and will not peel away in the pan.
Heat a good depth of oil over medium heat. Too hot and the panko burns before the meat is cooked.
Cook 5 min a side, untouched for the first two minutes, to an even golden colour.
Drain on a rack rather than paper, which would soften the underside.
Shred the cabbage into fine threads and dress it with mayonnaise let down with soy, just before serving.
n10: Take the beef out 20 min ahead and dry it: cold, damp meat greys instead of searing.
Cook the cubed potatoes 15 min in salted water, starting cold.
Boil the peas only 4 min: any longer and they lose their colour.
Drain and crush them roughly with a fork along with the butter, chopped mint and lemon juice.
Keep the texture uneven: a smooth purée would lose the whole point of the dish.
Heat a pan until it smokes and sear the beef 3 min a side without moving it.
Lift it out and rest it 4 min on a board, loosely covered. The juices redistribute during that rest.
Slice across the grain and serve on the crushed peas, with the potatoes.
n11: Crack the eggs into a bowl and beat them with a fork, not a whisk: you want them mixed, not aerated.
Add the chopped herbs and salt now, which helps the proteins relax.
Heat a non-stick pan over medium heat, never high: an omelette burnt outside and raw inside always comes from too fierce a flame.
Melt the butter and wait for it to foam without colouring.
Pour in the eggs, let them set 30 seconds, then draw the edges to the centre with a spatula while tilting the pan.
Repeat for 3 min, until only a film of liquid remains on the surface.
Scatter the grated comté, fold the omelette in half and cut the heat: it finishes on its own warmth.
Serve at once with the dressed salad and bread.
n12: Slice the pork into 5 mm strips, across the grain.
Toss it with the spices and a pinch of salt and leave 10 min while you prepare the rest.
Slice the red onion very finely and cover it with the lime juice. It turns pink and loses its bite within 10 min.
Heat a pan until it smokes and spread the pork in a single layer.
Leave it 3 min untouched, until it caramelises, then stir and continue 5 min.
Cook in two batches if the pan is small: crowded, the pork boils in its juices instead of roasting.
Warm the tortillas 30 seconds a side in a dry pan and stack them in a cloth to stay supple.
Fill at the table: pork, pickled onion, cream and coriander.
n13: Press the tofu 15 min between two plates with a weight: it is the water in it that stops it browning.
Cut it into 2 cm cubes and dry them again on kitchen paper.
Soak the noodles 8 min in warm water, then rinse under cold water and oil them lightly.
Heat the wok very hot, add the oil and spread the tofu in a single layer. Do not touch it for 4 min.
Turn it and continue 4 min: it should be golden on at least two faces.
Add the grated carrot for 2 min, then the noodles, soy and sesame oil, and toss 2 min.
Cut the heat before adding the bean sprouts: cooked, they lose the crunch that is their whole point.
Crushed peanuts and lime as you serve.
n14: Heat the oven to 200 °C. Slice the potatoes into 3 mm rounds, on a mandoline if you have one.
Toss them with the oil, sliced garlic and salt, and spread them in a single layer in a dish.
Roast them 15 min alone: they need the head start, as the fish cooks three times faster.
Take the dish out, add the whole cherry tomatoes, the olives and the oregano, and fold together.
Dry the cod fillets, salt them and lay them on the vegetables.
Back in the oven for 12 min. The fish is done when a knife tip parts the flakes without resistance.
The tomatoes should have burst: their juice mingles with the oil and makes the sauce.
Serve straight from the dish, with a thread of raw oil.
n15: Heat a litre of stock and keep it simmering beside the pan throughout.
Sweat the chopped shallots 3 min in butter over low heat, without colour.
Add the rice and toast it 2 min: the grains turn translucent at the edges and stay opaque at the centre.
Deglaze with white wine and let it evaporate completely, 2 min.
Add the stock a ladle at a time, waiting for each to be absorbed, stirring often.
Allow 16 min, then add the peas straight from frozen for the last 5 min.
Taste: the grain must stay firm at the core. Cut the heat and beat in cold butter and parmesan vigorously.
Add the chopped mint at the very last moment, off the heat: heated, it blackens and loses its scent.
n16: Cube the bread to 2 cm and fry 8 min in a pan with a little oil, stirring regularly.
Flatten the chicken breasts slightly so they are of even thickness, and salt them.
Sear 6 min a side over medium-high heat, without moving them until they release on their own.
Rest 5 min before slicing: cut straight away, they lose their juices onto the plate.
Make the dressing by blending mayonnaise, mustard, lemon juice, anchovies and garlic to a smooth emulsion.
The anchovies do not taste of anchovy in the finished dressing: they bring the savoury depth that makes a Caesar.
Wash and dry the lettuce thoroughly. A wet leaf holds no dressing.
Assemble at the last moment: leaves, dressing, sliced chicken, croutons and shaved parmesan.
n17: Chop the turkey with a knife into small pieces rather than buying it minced: the texture is far better.
Heat a casserole over high heat and spread the meat untouched for 3 min so it colours.
Break it up, add the diced onion and pepper, and continue 5 min.
Add the cumin and paprika off the heat and stir 1 min: spices need hot fat, not flame.
Pour in the chopped tomatoes and the drained, rinsed kidney beans.
Crush a ladle of beans against the side to thicken the chilli naturally.
Simmer 15 min uncovered, stirring now and then, and cook the rice alongside.
Taste and adjust: white meat needs more salt and spice than red.
n18: Soak the noodles 8 min in warm, not boiling, water and drain without rinsing.
Slice the chicken finely and separate the cabbage ribs from its leaves: they do not cook at the same rate.
Mix the soy, fish sauce and sugar in a bowl: a stir-fry leaves no time to measure mid-cook.
Heat the wok until it smokes, add the oil and sear the chicken 4 min with the garlic, without stirring for the first minute.
Push it aside, crack the eggs into the clear space and scramble 30 seconds.
Add the cabbage ribs for 1 min, then the leaves and the noodles.
Pour the sauce down the scorching sides of the wok rather than onto the food: it caramelises instead of diluting.
Toss 2 min, lifting with the spatula rather than stirring, and serve at once.
n19: Drain and rinse the chickpeas, then dry them in a cloth: wet, the patties would not hold.
Crush them with a fork, not a processor: whole pieces need to survive for the texture.
Add the egg, breadcrumbs and cumin, mix and rest 15 min so the crumbs absorb the moisture.
Grate the cucumber and squeeze it hard in a cloth. That water is what ruins most tzatziki.
Mix it into the yoghurt with chopped mint, a little garlic and lemon, and chill.
Shape six patties about 1.5 cm thick, with damp hands.
Cook 4 min a side over medium heat in a film of oil, without turning them too early or they break up.
Serve in warm pitta with the well-chilled tzatziki; the contrast makes the dish.
n20: Cover the bulgur with boiling salted water to a centimetre above, cover and leave 15 min to swell.
Grate the onion and squeeze it in your hand to remove excess juice.
Mix the lamb, grated onion, cumin and half the chopped mint, working it 1 min by hand.
Rest 15 min in the fridge: the mixture holds together far better afterwards.
Shape ten tightly packed balls between damp palms.
Brown them 8 min over medium heat by rolling them around the pan rather than turning them, so they colour all over.
Fluff the bulgur with a fork and toss with the diced tomato, lemon juice and the rest of the mint.
Serve the meatballs on the bulgur, with salted yoghurt on the side.
n21: Rinse and pick over the lentils, without soaking them.
Cook them 20 min in the stock with the diced carrot and the sliced onion, unsalted.
Salt added at the start toughens lentil skins and lengthens the cooking.
Meanwhile prick the sausages and brown them 8 min over medium heat in a pan, with no added fat.
Lift them out and cut into thick rounds, keeping the rendered fat in the pan.
Drain the lentils keeping a little broth, and return them to the pan.
Add the mustard slackened with the vinegar and a little broth, and fold off the heat: cooked mustard turns bitter.
Combine with the sausages and their fat, salt now, and scatter with parsley.
n22: Rinse the short-grain rice and cook it 15 min covered, then rest 10 min without opening.
Grate the carrot raw and leave it as it is: the contrast between raw and cooked is the principle of the Korean bowl.
Wilt the spinach 2 min in a pan, squeeze it and season with a drop of sesame oil and salt.
Heat a pan over high heat and spread the mince untouched for 3 min so it caramelises.
Break it up, add the garlic, soy and half the gochujang, and continue 3 min.
Fry the eggs in hot oil: the edges should brown and frill while the yolk stays running.
Put the rice in the bowls and arrange each topping in its own section, unmixed.
Sit the egg in the middle and serve the rest of the gochujang separately: it is mixed at the table.
n23: Heat the oven to 210 °C and lift the halloumi out of its brine to drain.
Cut the courgette, pepper and red onion into large 3 cm pieces of even size.
Toss them in a bowl with the oil and oregano rather than drizzling in the tray: the coating is far more even.
Spread on a tray without crowding and roast 20 min.
Add the whole cherry tomatoes and fold through, then lay the halloumi over in 1 cm slices.
Return for 8 min: halloumi should brown without melting, being a cheese that holds its shape.
Take the tray out and squeeze the lemon straight onto it; the steam lifts the caramelised bits.
Serve with warm pitta, scooping up every bit of juice from the tray.
n24: Heat the stock and coconut milk together with the sliced ginger, never reaching a boil.
A coconut broth that boils splits for good: it should only tremble at the surface.
Infuse 5 min so the ginger flavours it, then add the sliced mushrooms for 5 min.
Slice the chicken very thinly and slip it into the simmering broth.
Poach it 6 min only: white meat poached too long turns stringy.
Cook the noodles separately and divide between bowls, so they do not cloud the broth.
Season off the heat: fish sauce for salt, the juice of two limes for acidity.
Taste and adjust both until balanced, then add whole coriander leaves as you serve.
n25: Split the sausage skins and squeeze the meat straight into a hot pan, breaking it up.
Let it colour 6 min without stirring much, to get uneven, well-browned pieces.
Slice the fennel very finely, core included, and keep the green fronds for the end.
Add it with the crushed garlic and cook 5 min: it should turn tender and lose its crunch.
Pour in the chopped tomatoes and the chilli and simmer 10 min over medium heat.
Cook the pasta a minute under and keep a ladle of the cooking water.
Finish it 1 min in the pan with some of that water: the starch binds sauce to pasta.
Parmesan and chopped fennel fronds off the heat.
n26: The rice must be cold and dry, cooked the day before. Hot rice sticks and crushes under the spatula.
Separate the grains by hand before you start.
Drain the kimchi keeping its juice, and cut it roughly with scissors.
Heat the wok very hot, add the oil and stir-fry the kimchi 3 min: cooking concentrates its flavour and softens its acidity.
Add the rice, pressing it with the spatula to break it up, then stir-fry 4 min without stopping.
Pour the soy and two spoonfuls of kimchi juice down the scorching sides of the wok rather than onto the rice.
Fry the eggs separately in hot oil, frilled edges and running yolk.
Plate the rice, sit the egg on top, add sesame and spring onions.
n27: Peel the potatoes and start them in cold salted water, 18 min, until a knife passes through without resistance.
Drain them and dry them 1 min over the switched-off heat: that evaporation prevents a watery mash.
Crush them with a fork along with the butter, deliberately leaving lumps.
Dry the hake fillets and salt them, then set out three plates: flour, beaten egg, breadcrumbs.
Coat, pressing well, then rest 10 min in the fridge so the coating adheres.
Cook 4 min a side over medium heat in a film of fat, untouched for the first two minutes.
The fish is done when the coating is golden and the flesh flakes at a knife tip.
Serve with the crushed potatoes, chopped parsley and a lemon wedge.
n28: Wash the spinach and spin it thoroughly dry: residual water would stop the sauce thickening.
Sweat the sliced onion and garlic 5 min over low heat with the cumin, until translucent.
Add the spinach in large handfuls, waiting for each to wilt before adding the next.
Cook 4 min, then let the released water evaporate for 3 min uncovered.
The base should be moist but with no free liquid, or the eggs would boil instead of poaching.
Make four well-spaced wells and crack the eggs in, salting the yolks.
Cover and cook 6 min over low heat: the white set, the yolk still running.
Crumble the feta, squeeze the lemon and serve from the pan with warm pitta.
n29: Rinse the lentils and cook them 20 min in three times their volume of unsalted water.
Salt right at the end, then drain and let them cool to warm rather than cold.
Warm lentils absorb dressing; cold ones let it slide off.
Chop the shallot very finely and leave it 5 min in the balsamic vinegar, which softens it.
Add the mustard then the oil in a stream, whisking to emulsify.
Toss the warm lentils with the dressing and rest 10 min so they take it up.
Dice the beetroot and add it at the last moment: folded in early, it stains everything pink.
Crumble the goat's cheese over and scatter with walnuts toasted 3 min dry.
n30: Boil the potatoes 18 min in salted water and the green beans 8 min, refreshing them at once to fix the colour.
Dry the chicken breasts and salt them. Dry meat sears; wet meat blanches.
Sear 6 min a side over medium-high heat, without moving them until they release on their own.
Keep them warm under a sheet of paper, not tightly covered.
Sweat the chopped shallots 3 min in the same pan, scraping up the sticky bits.
Deglaze with white wine and reduce almost to dry, 3 min: this is what concentrates the flavour.
Add the cream and mustard off the heat, then return to low heat for 2 min. Boiled mustard turns bitter.
Return the chicken and its juices to the sauce, and serve with the vegetables.
n31: Heat 700 ml water with the sliced mushrooms and infuse 5 min just below a simmer.
Never boil it: miso is a living product that fierce heat destroys.
Take a ladle of that broth into a bowl and slacken the miso into it with a fork until perfectly smooth.
Pour it back into the pan off the heat, stirring gently.
Cook the udon separately per the packet and rinse them briefly to wash off excess starch.
Add the spinach to the hot broth: it wilts in 1 min with no further cooking.
Divide the noodles between bowls and pour the miso broth over.
Finish with sesame oil, soy and spring onions, and serve without waiting.
n32: Drain and rinse the kidney beans, then dry them lightly.
Fry the sliced onion 5 min, add the cumin and chilli and stir 1 min.
Add the beans and crush them with a fork against the base of the pan, to a thick purée.
Cook 5 min more until it holds together: too loose and it would soak through the tortilla.
Fill one half of each tortilla, leaving a centimetre border, and cover with cheddar.
Fold over and press lightly with your palm to seal.
Cook 3 min a side in a dry pan over medium heat, pressing with a spatula.
Rest 2 min before cutting into wedges: the cheese firms up and the filling stays in.
n33: Slice the chorizo into rounds and brown them 3 min in a dry pan over medium heat.
It releases a red, scented fat: keep it and lift the rounds out.
Fry the sliced pepper and onion 6 min in that fat.
Add the chopped tomatoes and the paprika and reduce 6 min over medium heat.
In a second pan, brown the gnocchi 6 min straight from the pack, stirring little.
They need to form a crust: that is the difference between pan-fried gnocchi and boiled ones.
Combine everything with the chorizo and toss 1 min over high heat.
Chopped parsley off the heat, and serve while the gnocchi are still crisp.
n34: Heat the oven to 220 °C: a high temperature is needed for the aubergine flesh to collapse.
Halve the aubergines and score the flesh in a diamond pattern 1 cm deep without piercing the skin.
Brush them generously with oil: the cuts carry it right to the centre.
Roast 20 min cut side up, until the flesh sinks and turns creamy.
Mix the miso, honey and rice vinegar to a smooth, glossy paste.
Brush it over the aubergines and return for 8 min. Watch them: sweetened miso burns quickly.
Cook the short-grain rice alongside and rest it 10 min covered.
Scatter with sesame and chopped spring onions, and serve with the rice.
n35: Rinse the quinoa in cold water, rubbing it between your hands: its natural saponin is bitter.
