Cook it 13 min in twice its volume of salted water, then rest 5 min covered.
Spread it on a wide plate to cool fast: left in a heap it keeps cooking and turns pasty.
Dice the cucumber and halve the cherry tomatoes; salt the cucumber separately 10 min then pat dry.
Chop the parsley and mint finely and generously: the herbs are the main ingredient here.
Make a lemon and oil dressing, sharper than usual as the quinoa absorbs it.
Toss the cooled quinoa, the vegetables, the herbs and the sliced spring onions.
Crumble the feta in at the very last moment, or it breaks down and whitens the whole salad.
n36: Rinse the red lentils until the water runs clear: they foam far less afterwards.
Sweat the sliced onion 4 min, then add the grated ginger for 1 min.
Add the curry powder and warm it 1 min in the fat: dry spices only release their scent on contact with fat.
Pour in the lentils, the coconut milk and 200 ml water, stirring to lift the base.
Simmer 15 min over low heat, stirring regularly: red lentils catch very easily.
Add the diced tomatoes halfway through, which brings acidity without breaking down completely.
The dhal is ready when the lentils have collapsed and a spoon leaves a clean trail.
Salt only now, add the coriander off the heat, and serve with the rice.
p01: Peel the carrots and cut into 3 cm lengths. Split the leeks, rinse under water to wash out the grit, and cut into thick rounds.
Put the chicken in a casserole, cover with cold water and add the stock cubes. Bring to a bare simmer and skim off the grey foam that rises for the first 5 minutes.
Add the carrots and leeks and simmer 35 min covered, barely bubbling. The chicken should fall off the bone without resistance.
Meanwhile slice the mushrooms and fry 6 min in butter over high heat, leaving them alone for the first minute so they colour instead of weeping.
Lift out the chicken and vegetables, strain the broth and keep 600 ml.
Make a white roux: melt the remaining butter, add the flour and stir 2 min without letting it colour. Pour in the hot broth all at once, whisking, and cook 5 min until the sauce coats a spoon.
Off the heat, slacken the egg yolk with the cream and stir it in. Do not let it boil again or the liaison will split.
Return the chicken, vegetables and mushrooms, add the tarragon and a squeeze of lemon. Serve with the rice.
p02: Peel the potatoes, cut into even large chunks and start them in cold salted water, 20 min.
Meanwhile poach the fish 6 min in 400 ml of barely simmering milk, never boiling. Lift it out as soon as it flakes and keep the milk.
Wilt the spinach 3 min in a pan, then press it between two plates to drive out the water, or the bake will be swamped.
Make a béchamel: 30 g butter, the flour, 2 min of cooking, then the poaching milk in three additions, whisking. Cook 5 min, add nutmeg and salt.
Drain the potatoes, dry them 1 min over the switched-off heat, then mash with the remaining butter and hot milk.
Flake the fish into the béchamel and fold in the spinach and chopped dill.
Tip into a dish, cover with the mash, dragging a fork over it to make ridges that will brown, and scatter with gruyère.
Bake 25 min at 190 °C, then 3 min under the grill if the top is still pale.
p03: The day before if you can: cut the beef into large 4 cm cubes and marinate it cold in the wine with thyme, bay and a strip of orange zest.
Drain the meat and dry it thoroughly on kitchen paper. Wet meat does not colour, it boils.
Sear the cubes in two batches in a very hot casserole, 3 min a side, until a deep brown crust forms. Set aside.
Lower the heat and sweat the sliced onions and carrots 8 min, then add the crushed garlic for 1 min.
Dust with flour, stir 2 min, then pour in the strained marinade and the tomatoes. Scrape the base of the pot clean.
Return the meat and add the orange zest. The liquid should come level with the meat, not cover it.
Cover and simmer 2 h over very low heat, or in the oven at 150 °C. Stir once an hour.
Add the olives 15 min before the end. Serve on the polenta. A daube is better reheated the next day.
p04: Slice the onions very finely, on a mandoline if you have one: even thickness is what makes this work.
Put them in a large pan with the oil, thyme and bay, over low heat, with a lid resting on top.
Let them melt for 45 min, stirring every 10 min. They should turn blond and jammy, never brown or dry. Add a spoonful of water if they catch.
Take the lid off for the last 10 min to drive off the remaining moisture. The confit must stop releasing liquid.
Heat the oven to 200 °C. Roll out the pastry on its paper and prick the base with a fork.
Spread the cooled onions leaving a 1 cm border, lay the anchovies in a lattice and put an olive in each diamond.
Bake 25 min: the underside must be golden and dry.
Let it settle 10 min before cutting, or the topping slides off. Serve with the salad.
p05: In an ovenproof casserole, brown the belly pork cut into lardons for 5 min over medium heat with no added fat: it renders its own.
Add the chicken and sausages and colour them 8 min on all sides. Set everything aside.
In the same fat, sweat the diced onions and carrots 8 min, then the garlic for 1 min.
Pour in the tomatoes and thyme, scrape up the sticky bits and reduce 5 min.
Add the drained and rinsed beans, then the meats. Top up with water until it just comes level.
Bake uncovered 40 min. Halfway through, break the crust that has formed by pushing it under with a spoon: that is what builds the texture.
Scatter with breadcrumbs and give it 10 more minutes for a golden top.
p06: Halve the squash and scoop out the seeds. There is no need to peel it, the skin melts away. Cut into 1.5 cm cubes.
Roast half the cubes 20 min at 200 °C with a little oil: these go on top and keep some bite.
Heat 1 litre of stock and keep it at a simmer beside you. Cold stock would stall the cooking with every ladleful.
Sweat the shallots 4 min in butter, add the rest of the squash and the rice. Stir 2 min until the grains turn translucent at the edges.
Deglaze with white wine and let it evaporate completely, about 2 min.
Add the stock one ladle at a time, waiting for each to be absorbed. Allow 18 min and stir often: it is the friction between grains that releases the starch.
Taste: the rice should stay firm at the centre. Cut the heat, beat in cold butter and parmesan vigorously to bind.
Cover 2 min, then serve topped with the roasted cubes, crushed walnuts and fried sage.
p07: Cut the broccoli into very small florets and slice the stalks thinly, they are excellent.
Toast the breadcrumbs 3 min in a dry pan with a spoonful of oil and set aside: this is the crunch of the dish.
Bring a large pan of salted water to the boil. Drop in the broccoli for 4 min and lift it out with a slotted spoon.
Cook the pasta in the same water according to the packet.
Meanwhile warm the oil gently with the sliced garlic and the anchovies. Crush the anchovies with a spoon; they must dissolve completely within 3 min.
Add the broccoli and crush it roughly with a fork so it coats the pasta.
Drain the pasta keeping a ladle of water, tip it into the pan with a splash of that water and toss 1 min over high heat.
Serve with the chilli, parmesan and toasted crumbs over the top.
p08: Cut the aubergines into 2 cm cubes, salt them in a colander and leave 20 min. Pat dry: they will drink far less oil.
Fry them in two batches in hot oil, 8 min a batch, until golden and yielding. Drain on paper.
Blanch the celery in lengths for 3 min in boiling water to take off its bitterness.
In the same pan, melt the sliced onions 8 min over medium heat.
Add the celery, tomatoes, olives, rinsed capers and raisins. Simmer 15 min uncovered.
Make the sweet and sour: dissolve the sugar in the vinegar, pour it into the pan and let it evaporate 3 min over high heat. This is what defines a caponata.
Return the aubergines and fold gently so they don't break up, then cut the heat.
Let it cool completely before serving, with the toasted pine nuts. It is much better the next day and keeps 5 days.
p09: Break the spaghetti into 3 cm lengths. Toast them dry for 4 min in a large pan until they turn blond: this is what gives a fideuà its flavour.
Set them aside and prepare 700 ml of very hot stock with the saffron infusing in it.
Sear the squid rings 2 min over high heat and set aside. They toughen if overcooked.
Fry the finely diced onion and pepper 8 min, then add the garlic and paprika off the heat for 1 min so it doesn't burn.
Pour in the tomatoes and reduce 5 min until the mixture darkens and pulls away from the base.
Add the toasted pasta, stir, then pour in all the stock. Spread it evenly and do not stir again from this point.
Cook 12 min over medium heat. Lay the prawns and squid on top for the last 5 min.
Raise the heat for 1 min at the end to form a light crust underneath, then rest 5 min off the heat. Serve with the lemon.
p10: Cut the pork into even 3 cm cubes so they all cook at the same rate.
Make the marinade: juice of one lemon, crushed garlic, oregano, olive oil, salt, pepper. Roll the meat in it and leave at least 20 min at room temperature.
Meanwhile grate the cucumber and squeeze it hard in a cloth. The water it holds would ruin the tzatziki.
Mix the squeezed cucumber into the yoghurt with a little garlic and lemon, and chill.
Slice the red onion very finely and leave it 10 min in the juice of the second lemon: it loses its bite and turns pink.
Thread the meat onto skewers without packing it tight, so the heat can circulate.
Cook 10 min in a very hot pan or under the grill, turning a quarter turn every 2 to 3 min. The meat should be coloured outside and just opaque within.
Warm the pitta 1 min and fill with meat, tomato, onion and tzatziki.
p11: Put the chicken in a casserole with the sliced onions, the spices, 200 ml water and a knob of butter. Cover and cook 40 min over low heat.
Lift out the chicken, let it cool a little, then shred it by hand, discarding skin and bones.
Reduce the cooking juices uncovered for 10 min: they should become an almost dry onion compote.
Off the heat, pour in the beaten eggs and stir constantly for 3 min, like scrambled eggs. They bind the filling.
Mix the shredded chicken, the compote, the coriander and a squeeze of lemon. Taste and adjust: the filling should be assertively seasoned.
Toast the almonds 5 min in a pan and crush them with a little cinnamon and sugar.
Butter a tin and lay 5 filo sheets in a star, buttering each. Add the filling, scatter the almonds, fold the sheets in and cover with 2 more buttered sheets.
Bake 30 min at 190 °C until deeply golden and crisp. Dust with icing sugar and cinnamon as it comes out.
p12: Start the eggs in barely simmering water for 10 min, then cool under cold water and peel.
Cut the aubergines lengthways into 1 cm slices, salt them and leave 15 min.
Pat dry and fry 4 min a side in hot oil, until golden and completely soft at the centre.
Make the tahini sauce: slacken the tahini with lemon juice and cold water, a spoonful at a time. It will seize first and then turn smooth again, which is normal. Season.
Dice the tomatoes and cucumber small, mix with chopped parsley, and salt only just before serving.
Open the pitta and warm them 1 min in a dry pan.
Fill in this order: a spoon of tahini, the aubergines, sliced egg, the diced salad.
Finish with a streak of harissa and more tahini. Eaten by hand, warm or cold.
p13: Mix the yoghurt, half the spices, the grated garlic and ginger, and the lemon juice. Marinate the cubed chicken in it for 30 min, longer if you have time.
Drain the pieces without wiping them and sear 5 min over very high heat in a little butter, in two batches. They should char in places without cooking through.
Set the chicken aside. Lower the heat and melt the rest of the butter in the same pan.
Add the remaining spices and warm them 1 min: they should smell strong, which is the sign they have woken up.
Pour in the tomatoes, scrape the base, and reduce 20 min over medium heat until the oil rises to the surface.
Blend the sauce smooth with a stick blender; this is what sets the dish apart.
Return the chicken, add the cream and simmer 10 min over low heat without boiling.
Correct with a pinch of sugar if the tomatoes are sharp. Coriander to serve, with the rice.
p14: Rinse the lentils until the water runs clear.
Cook them in 800 ml water with the turmeric, 20 min over medium heat. Skim the foam of the first few minutes.
Meanwhile cut all the vegetables to an even size, about 2 cm.
When the lentils collapse, whisk them roughly to thicken the broth.
Add the carrots and aubergine, cook 10 min, then the courgette and tomatoes for 8 min more.
Make the tempering, the step that makes this dish: heat the oil in a small pan and throw in the coriander and cumin seeds. They should crackle within seconds.
Add the sliced onion and the chilli, fry 4 min until coloured, then pour the whole lot into the sambar. Stand back, it will spit.
Simmer 5 min together and finish with lemon juice. Serve with the rice.
p15: Chop the pork with a knife rather than blitzing it: the texture stays far more interesting.
Build the sauce in the bottom of two bowls: tahini, soy, vinegar, sesame oil, grated garlic and ginger, chilli paste. Loosen with 4 spoonfuls of hot water to the texture of pouring cream.
Heat a dry pan very hot. Add the pork and spread it out without touching it for 2 min so it catches.
Break it up with a spatula and cook 5 min more, until dry and crisp in places. This is where the flavour is made.
Deglaze with a spoonful of soy and set aside.
Blanch the shredded Chinese cabbage 2 min in the pasta water and lift it out.
Cook the noodles per the packet, draining but keeping a little of the water.
Lay the hot noodles on the sauce without mixing, add pork, cabbage, spring onions and crushed peanuts. You stir it all together at the table.
p16: Rinse the rice in cold water until it runs clear, then cook 15 min covered and leave it 10 min without lifting the lid.
Cut the chicken into 2 cm pieces and slice the onion thinly.
In a small pan, combine 150 ml water, the stock, soy, mirin and sugar. Bring to a simmer.
Add the onion and cook 3 min until translucent.
Add the chicken in a single layer and poach 6 min over medium heat, turning halfway.
Beat the eggs very roughly, leaving whites and yolks still distinct: this is what gives the dish its marbled look.
Pour two thirds of the egg over the chicken in a spiral, cover and cook 1 min. Add the rest and cover for another 30 seconds.
Cut the heat while the egg is still loose; it finishes setting on the hot rice. Slide onto the rice bowl and top with spring onions.
p17: Soak the noodles 20 min in warm water, then cook 6 min and rinse under cold water.
Cut them roughly with scissors and toss immediately with a spoonful of sesame oil and soy so they don't stick.
The Korean method cooks each vegetable separately, to keep its texture and colour. It costs ten extra minutes and changes everything.
Blanch the spinach 40 seconds, refresh, squeeze dry and season with garlic, sesame and salt.
Stir-fry the carrot in fine batons 2 min and set aside. Then the pepper 2 min, then the onion 3 min, then the mushrooms 4 min over high heat.
Make a very thin omelette with the beaten eggs, roll it and cut into ribbons.
Make the sauce with the remaining soy, sugar and sesame oil.
Combine everything in a large bowl and mix with your hands, the only way to coat without breaking things. Serve warm or cold, with the sesame seeds.
p18: Make the marinade: blend the spices, garlic, vinegar, orange juice and two slices of pineapple to a smooth paste. Pineapple contains an enzyme that tenderises the meat.
Slice the pork into 1 cm escalopes and coat them in the marinade. Leave 1 h in the fridge, not much longer, or the meat goes mushy.
Stack the slices on top of one another in a dish, packed tight, with pineapple rings between. This is the home version of the vertical spit.
Roast 40 min, basting twice with the rendered juices.
Take it out, rest 10 min, then slice the stack into thin strips across the layers.
Sear those strips 3 min in a very hot pan to caramelise the edges. This step is what makes real pastor.
Warm the tortillas 30 seconds a side in a dry pan, fill with the meat, red onion and coriander, lime on the side.
p19: Cut the chicken into large pieces and the chorizo into thick rounds.
Brown the chorizo 4 min in a casserole: it releases a red fat that will flavour the whole dish.
Sear the chicken in that fat 6 min on all sides, then set aside with the chorizo.
Add the diced onion, peppers and celery, the aromatic base of Cajun cooking. Sweat them 8 min until they collapse.
Add the spices and thyme, stir 1 min, then the tomatoes. Reduce 5 min.
Tip in the rice and stir 2 min to coat it well, then add 700 ml hot stock and the meats.
Bring to a simmer, cover and cook 20 min over very low heat without ever stirring, or the rice turns sticky.
Cut the heat, rest 10 min covered, then fluff with a fork. Spring onions to serve.
p20: Cut the beef into 4 cm cubes. A braising cut is essential; a lean one would turn dry.
Open the coconut milk without shaking it and skim off the thick cream from the top.
Heat that cream alone in a casserole for 5 min, until it splits and the oil beads on the surface. This is the foundation of any Thai curry.
Fry the curry paste in it for 3 min, stirring: it should darken and smell fragrant.
Add the meat and coat it for 3 min, then pour in the rest of the coconut milk, the cinnamon and 200 ml water.
Simmer 1 h 15 covered, on the lowest heat. The meat should give way to a spoon.
Add the potatoes and onions in large pieces and cook 25 min more uncovered so the sauce thickens.
Season at the end: fish sauce for salt, brown sugar, lime juice. Taste and adjust all three until it balances. Toasted peanuts to serve.
p21: Toast the raw rice dry in a pan for 6 min over medium heat, stirring, until golden brown and fragrant.
Grind it to a coarse powder in a mortar or grinder. This powder is the signature of larb: it thickens and adds crunch.
Chop the chicken finely with a knife, not in a food processor.
Cook it in a pan with only 3 spoonfuls of water and no fat, 6 min over medium heat, breaking up the pieces. You poach it rather than sear it.
Cut the heat as soon as no pink remains, and let it cool 5 min.
Slice the shallots, spring onions and chilli very finely.
Mix the warm chicken with lime juice, fish sauce, shallots and chilli. Taste: it should be assertively sour and salty.
Add the chopped herbs and the rice powder just before serving, or it softens. Serve in lettuce leaves.
p22: Take the meat out 30 min ahead: meat at room temperature sears better than cold meat.
Cut it into 4 cm cubes, dry it, and dust lightly with flour, tapping off the excess.
Sear in three batches in hot butter, 4 min a batch. Never crowd the pot, or the meat releases its water and boils.
Set the meat aside and melt the sliced onions 12 min over medium heat with the brown sugar, until they caramelise.
Deglaze with the beer, scraping up every sticky bit from the base: that is where the flavour lives.
Return the meat, add the carrots, thyme and bay. The liquid should come level with the meat.
Spread a large slice of bread generously with mustard and lay it mustard side down on the surface of the stew. It melts in and thickens the sauce.
Cover and simmer 2 h over very low heat. Serve with steamed potatoes.
p23: Make the stuffing: blend the parsley, garlic, chilli, a little salt and oil to a green paste.
Score the fish fillets and push some of the paste inside. Leave 15 min.
Fry the sliced onions 8 min in the oil over medium heat, in a large casserole.
Add the tomato purée and cook it 4 min, stirring. It should darken and lose its metallic edge, a step too often skipped.
Pour in the chopped tomatoes and 1.2 litres of water and bring to a simmer.
Add the vegetables in large pieces, the hardest first: carrots and sweet potato 10 min, then the cabbage 10 min. Lift each out as it is done and keep warm.
Poach the fish 10 min in that broth and lift it out carefully.
Measure the remaining broth, keep two parts for one part rice, and cook the rice in it 20 min covered. Serve the rice, vegetables and fish, lemon on the side.
p24: Make the pastry: rub the flour and cold diced butter together with your fingertips, add 1 egg, a pinch of salt and 120 ml cold water. Knead just enough to come together.
Wrap and rest 30 min in the fridge. Rested pastry does not shrink in the oven.
Meanwhile sweat the finely diced onions and pepper for 10 min.
Add the mince, break it up with a spatula and cook 8 min until well browned.
Add the spices, raisins and chopped olives, then 100 ml water. Simmer 10 min then cool completely. A hot filling would make the pastry soggy.
Roll the pastry to 3 mm and cut out 12 cm discs.
Put a spoon of filling on each, wet the edge, fold over and seal by crimping or rolling the edge onto itself.
Brush with beaten egg and bake 25 min at 200 °C until well coloured.
p25: Shred the cabbage finely and blanch it 5 min in boiling salted water, then drain.
Render the belly pork cut into lardons, 6 min over medium heat in a casserole.
Add the sliced sausages and brown 4 min, then set everything aside.
Sweat the onions 6 min in the fat, add the sliced mushrooms and raise the heat for 5 min to colour them.
Add the cabbage, the grated apples and the chopped apricots, and stir 3 min.
Pour in the tomatoes, paprika and bay, return the meats, and add water to come level.
Cover and simmer 40 min over low heat, stirring now and then. The cabbage should turn soft and the whole thing take on a red-brown colour.
Taste and adjust the sourness. Serve with steamed potatoes. Bigos improves on reheating.
p26: Take the chicken out of the fridge 45 min ahead. Dry it carefully, the skin especially: this is the condition for crisp skin.
Heat the oven to 200 °C. Season the cavity and the outside generously and tuck thyme inside.
Separate the garlic cloves without peeling them. In their skins they confit rather than burn.
Colour the chicken 10 min on all sides in a casserole with the butter, turning it with two wooden spoons so as not to pierce the skin.
Arrange the garlic, the potatoes in large pieces and the herbs around it, and pour over the white wine.
Cover and roast 1 h 10, basting with the juices every 20 min.
Take the lid off for the last 15 min to bring the skin back to crispness.
Rest 10 min before carving, to let the juices redistribute. Squash the confit garlic onto toast.
p27: Choose waxy potatoes and peel them. Slice into 3 mm rounds, on a mandoline for preference: evenness is everything here.
Do not rinse them. It is their starch that binds the gratin, and rinsing it away gives a watery dish.
Rub a dish with a cut garlic clove, then butter it generously.
Heat the milk and cream with the remaining crushed garlic, nutmeg, salt and pepper, without boiling.
Slide the rounds in and cook 10 min over low heat, stirring gently. The mixture should thicken slightly.
Transfer to the dish, spreading evenly; the liquid should just come level with the surface.
Bake 1 h at 160 °C. Slow, gentle cooking is what separates a real dauphinois from a failed gratin.
Test with a knife tip: it should pass through without resistance. Rest 15 min before serving with the salad.
p28: Grill the whole peppers 15 min under the oven grill, turning them, until the skin blisters and blackens in places.
Shut them in a covered bowl for 10 min: the steam lifts the skin, which then slips off between your fingers. Cut into strips.
Meanwhile prick the merguez and cook them 8 min in a pan. Set aside and keep the rendered fat.
Melt the sliced onions 8 min in that fat, then add the garlic for 1 min.
Add the peeled and chopped tomatoes, the cumin and paprika. Reduce 15 min uncovered: the mixture should thicken and lose its water.
Fold in the pepper strips and the merguez cut into lengths, and simmer 5 min.
Make four wells, crack in the eggs and salt the yolks. Cover and cook 6 min: the white should be set and the yolk still runny.
Harissa and coriander to serve, with plenty of bread.
p29: Heat the oven to 210 °C. Cut the aubergines, courgettes and peppers into 2 cm pieces.
Spread them over two trays without crowding, oil, salt and roast 25 min. Crowded, they would steam rather than roast.
Meanwhile reduce the passata 15 min with the garlic and basil, until it coats a spoon.
Make the béchamel: butter and flour roux for 2 min, then the hot milk in three additions, whisking. Cook 6 min until thick, season, add nutmeg.
Drain the mozzarella and slice it. Wet mozzarella would make the dish watery.
Build it: a ladle of tomato sauce on the base, lasagne sheets, vegetables, béchamel, mozzarella. Repeat three times.
Finish with béchamel and all the parmesan, which forms the crust.
Bake 40 min at 180 °C. Cover with baking paper if the top browns too fast. Rest 15 min before cutting or the layers slide.
p30: Prepare everything before you light the heat: a stir-fry takes five minutes and there is no time to chop along the way.
Cut the carrot and pepper into fine batons, shred the cabbage, chop the garlic and ginger.
Cook the noodles 1 min less than the packet says, rinse under cold water and oil them lightly.
Heat a wok or large pan empty until a drop of water vanishes instantly. Add the oil.
Throw in the garlic and ginger for 20 seconds, then the carrot and pepper for 2 min, stirring constantly.
Push the vegetables aside, crack the eggs into the clear space and scramble 30 seconds before combining.
Add the cabbage for 1 min, then the noodles, soy and vinegar. Toss 2 min, lifting rather than stirring.
Cut the heat, add the bean sprouts and spring onions and a thread of sesame oil, and serve at once.
q01: Steep the sliced rounds of two lemons in coarse salt for 30 min: a shortcut to preserved lemon, which loses its bitterness this way.
Dry the chicken thighs and brown them 8 min in the oil, skin side down first, in a wide casserole. Set aside.
Sweat the sliced onions 10 min in the rendered fat over medium heat, until translucent.
Add the garlic, grated ginger and turmeric and stir 1 min off the heat so the spices do not burn.
Return the chicken, add 300 ml water and the herbs tied in a bundle. Cover and simmer 35 min over low heat.
Rinse the lemon slices and add them with the rinsed olives for the last 15 min.
Lift out the chicken and reduce the sauce 8 min uncovered: it should turn glossy and deep yellow.
Correct the acidity with the juice of the third lemon. Serve on the couscous with the chopped fresh herbs.
q02: Slice the leeks, fennel and onions. Sweat them 12 min over low heat in the oil without colouring: you want them soft, not browned.
Add the tomatoes, the cubed potatoes and 1.2 litres of water. Bring to a simmer.
Add the saffron and cook 25 min at a gentle bubble, until the potatoes crush against a fork.
Add the fish in pieces and cook only 8 min: overcooked, it toughens and makes the broth bitter.
Blend everything with a stick blender, then pass through a sieve, pressing hard with a ladle. It is the sieving that gives the velvety texture.
Make the rouille: crush two garlic cloves to a paste with salt, stir into the mayonnaise with the chilli and a spoonful of the hot soup.
Toast slices of bread and rub them with a raw garlic clove.
Serve the soup piping hot with the rouille, croutons and gruyère separately, so each person builds their own.
q03: Cut the beef into 5 cm cubes, larger than for a bourguignon: they cook a long time and will shrink.
Dry them thoroughly and sear in two batches in a very hot casserole, 4 min each, until brown-crusted.
Set the meat aside, lower the heat and sweat the sliced onions 8 min.
Dust with flour, stir 2 min, then deglaze with the white wine, scraping every sticky bit from the base.
Return the meat, add the stock, garlic, thyme, bay and a wide strip of orange zest. The liquid should come level.
Cover and simmer 1 h 30 on the lowest heat. The meat should begin to yield to a fork.
Add the carrots in large lengths and continue 45 min uncovered: they cook in the sauce as it reduces.
Remove the zest and herbs and taste. Serve with steamed potatoes. Better still the next day.
q04: Cut the aubergines into 2 cm cubes, salt them in a colander and drain 20 min.
Pat them very dry: surface water would make the oil spit and prevent browning.
Fry in two batches in hot oil, 8 min each, until golden and soft at the centre. Drain on paper.
In a pan, soften the crushed garlic 1 min in two spoonfuls of the frying oil.
Pour in the passata, salt, add a pinch of sugar if it is sharp, and reduce 20 min over medium heat.
The sauce is ready when it pulls away from the base of the pan leaving a clean trail.
Cook the pasta al dente and tip it into the sauce with a ladle of cooking water, tossing 1 min over high heat.
Fold in the aubergines and torn basil off the heat, then crumble the feta over at the table.
q05: Flatten the escalopes between two sheets of baking paper to 5 mm. Do not salt them: the ham does that.
Lay a slice of ham on each with a few sage leaves, and pin with a cocktail stick laid flat.
Flour only the meat side, tapping off the excess. The ham side stays bare so it does not go soft.
Heat half the butter over high heat and sear the escalopes 3 min ham side first, then 2 min on the other.
Keep them warm under a sheet of paper, not tightly covered, or the crust softens.
Deglaze the pan with white wine, scraping the base, and reduce by half, 3 min.
Cut the heat and finish the sauce with the remaining very cold butter, swirling the pan rather than whisking.
Wilt the spinach 3 min with garlic in another pan. Spoon the sauce over and add a squeeze of lemon.
q06: Peel the prawns keeping the shells if they have them: they make the stock.
Fry the shells 3 min in the oil, cover with a litre of water and the stock cubes, simmer 15 min and strain.
In a casserole, sweat the finely diced onion and pepper 10 min over medium heat.
Add the garlic and paprika off the heat and stir 30 seconds to avoid bitterness.
Pour in the tomatoes and reduce 5 min, until the mixture clearly darkens.
Add the rice, stir 2 min, then pour in 900 ml of scalding stock with the saffron. Unlike a paella, this should stay soupy: three parts liquid to one of rice.
Cook 16 min over medium heat uncovered, stirring occasionally.
Add the prawns for the last 3 min. Serve at once, as the rice keeps absorbing. Parsley and lemon at the last moment.
q07: Wilt the spinach in handfuls in a large pan, 5 min, until completely collapsed.
Tip into a colander and press by hand, then wring it in a cloth. This is the crucial step: one gram of excess water and the pastry stays soggy.
Chop it roughly with a knife and put it in a bowl.
Fry the sliced spring onions 3 min and add to the spinach with the crumbled feta, beaten eggs, dill, nutmeg and a squeeze of lemon.
Melt the butter. Lay a filo sheet in a buttered tin, brush it, and repeat with 5 sheets at offset angles.
Spread the filling, fold the overhang in, then cover with 4 buttered sheets, scrunching them slightly for texture.
Score the portions down to the filling before baking: afterwards the pastry would shatter under the knife.
Bake 45 min at 180 °C to an even deep gold. Rest 15 min before serving.
q08: Cut the potatoes into large wedges rather than small pieces: they need to confit in the juices without collapsing.
Make the marinade: juice of two lemons, oil, crushed garlic, oregano, mustard, salt and pepper, well emulsified.
Toss the potatoes with half the marinade in a large dish and coat the chicken in the rest.
Sit the chicken skin side up on the potatoes and pour 200 ml hot stock into the base of the dish.
Roast 45 min. The liquid should simmer: it cooks the potatoes from below while the skin roasts above.
Baste halfway, then continue 20 min uncovered to drive off the remaining liquid and colour everything.
Add the third lemon in slices for the last 10 min. Serve with the salad.
q09: Rinse the beans thoroughly: the canning liquid is salty and tastes metallic.
Sweat the finely sliced onions 10 min over low heat in the oil, until they melt.
Add the crushed garlic and cook 1 min without letting it colour.
Add the tomato purée and cook it 3 min, stirring constantly: it must darken, and that is what gives the dish its depth.
Add the cumin, paprika and chilli and stir 30 seconds off the heat to wake them without burning them.
Pour in the chopped tomatoes and 300 ml water and bring to a simmer.
Add the beans and simmer 25 min uncovered, crushing a ladleful against the side of the pan to thicken the sauce naturally.
Finish with lemon juice and coriander. Serve with plenty of bread. Keeps 5 days and improves on standing.
q10: Split the pitta through the middle and tear them into irregular pieces.
Toast 8 min at 190 °C with a little oil, until dry and brittle. They must stay crisp in the salad rather than go limp.
Flatten the chicken breasts slightly so they cook evenly and rub them with oil, sumac and salt.
Sear 6 min a side in a very hot pan without moving them, to get clean marks.
Rest 5 min before slicing: cut straight away, they would lose their juices.
Make the dressing: lemon juice, oil, crushed garlic, sumac, salt. The sumac brings the characteristic fruity sourness.
Cut the cucumber, tomatoes and onion into large pieces rather than small dice: fattoush is eaten in proper mouthfuls.
Toss the vegetables, chopped herbs and dressing, then add the bread and chicken at the very last moment.
q11: Cover the bulgur with cold water and leave 30 min to swell, then squeeze it firmly to extract all the water.
Make the filling: fry a sliced onion 6 min, add a third of the meat and cook 6 min.
Add the toasted pine nuts, the cinnamon and half the cumin, then set aside to cool.
Blend the rest of the meat with the two remaining onions, the squeezed bulgur, the cumin and salt, to a smooth sticky paste.
With wet hands, spread half this paste over the base of a buttered dish in an even 1.5 cm layer.
Spread the filling over, then cover with the rest of the paste, smoothing with a wet hand.
Score diamonds with a knife tip and pour the melted butter over the whole surface: it is what makes the crust.
Bake 40 min at 190 °C to a deep gold. Serve with the yoghurt, mint and lemon.
q12: Cut the lamb into 4 cm cubes keeping some fat: it is what gives the richness after two hours.
Heat the oil and throw in the cinnamon and coriander seeds for 30 seconds, until they crackle.
Sear the meat in two batches, 5 min each, until well coloured. Set aside.
Melt the finely sliced onions 15 min over medium heat: they must turn golden brown, which is the colour base of the dish.
Add the garlic and ginger paste and cook 2 min, then the paprika and garam masala for 1 min off the heat.
Stir in the yoghurt a spoonful at a time over low heat, without stopping. Added all at once it would split immediately.
Return the meat, add 200 ml water, cover and simmer 1 h 30 on the lowest heat.
Uncover for the last 20 min: the sauce should coat and the oil bead on the surface. Serve with the rice.
q13: Drain and rinse the chickpeas, setting a ladleful aside.
Heat the oil and fry the finely sliced onions 12 min: you need real brown colour, not mere translucency.
Add the grated garlic and ginger and cook 2 min until the raw smell goes.
Add the cumin, turmeric and chilli and stir 1 min in the hot oil.
Pour in the tomatoes and cook 12 min over medium heat, until the fat separates and rises at the edges.
Mash the reserved ladle of chickpeas with a fork and add it: it thickens the sauce without cream.
Add the rest of the chickpeas and 150 ml water, and simmer 12 min covered.
Off the heat, add the garam masala, lemon juice and coriander. Garam masala always goes in at the end.
q14: Cut the chicken into 1.5 cm cubes and mix with a spoonful of cornflour, one of soy and one of water. Leave 15 min: this is velveting, which keeps the meat tender over high heat.
Make the sauce in a bowl: the rest of the soy, the vinegar, sugar, remaining cornflour and 3 spoonfuls of water. Dissolve fully.
Cut everything and line it up within reach. The dish takes four minutes and nothing can wait.
Toast the peanuts 4 min in a dry pan and set aside.
Heat the wok empty until it just smokes, add the oil and sear the chicken 3 min without stirring at first, so it colours.
Push it aside and throw the garlic, ginger and chilli into the oil for 20 seconds, no more.
Pour in the sauce, stirring it first as the cornflour settles. It coats within 30 seconds.
Cut the heat, add the peanuts and spring onions, toss and serve at once on the rice.
q15: Cut the beef into 4 cm cubes and blanch them 5 min in boiling water, then rinse. This removes the impurities and clears the sauce.
Caramelise the brown sugar with two spoonfuls of water in a casserole to an amber colour, 3 min. Watch it, it burns fast.
Add the oil, the sliced ginger and the crushed garlic and stir 30 seconds.
Add the meat and coat it in the caramel for 3 min, stirring.
Pour in the soy sauce, the five spice and water to come only halfway up. Chinese braising uses little liquid.
Cover and simmer 1 h 30 on the lowest heat, turning the meat every 30 min.
Add the carrots in lengths and continue 25 min uncovered: the sauce should reduce to a syrup that lacquers the meat.
Finish with the rice vinegar, which lifts the whole thing. Raw spring onions on top, rice on the side.
q16: Rinse the rice until the water runs clear, cook 15 min covered and rest 10 min without opening.
Slice the beef as thinly as you possibly can, across the grain. Fifteen minutes in the freezer makes it far easier.
Slice the onions into 5 mm strips from top to root.
In a wide pan combine 150 ml water, the soy, mirin, sugar and grated ginger. Bring to a simmer.
Add the onions and cook 5 min until translucent and sweet.
Add the beef, separating the slices, and poach barely 3 min. Meat this thin cooks almost instantly.
Skim the grey foam that rises, which keeps the broth clean.
Serve over the rice with a ladle of broth, a raw egg yolk in the middle and the spring onions.
q17: Cut the chicken into 4 cm pieces, keeping irregular shapes: the corners become the crisp parts.
Mix the soy, mirin and grated ginger and garlic, and marinate the chicken 20 min. No longer, or the salt firms the flesh.
Cook the rice and shred the cabbage very finely meanwhile.
Drain the chicken without wiping it and roll it in the cornflour and flour mixture. The cornflour is what gives the light coating.
Heat the oil to 160 °C and fry once for 4 min. Drain on a rack and rest 5 min.
Raise the oil to 190 °C and fry again for 1 min 30. This double frying is the rule: the first cooks, the second crisps.
Drain on a rack, never on paper, which would soften the underside.
Salt as it comes out and serve at once with the rice, raw cabbage and lemony mayonnaise.
q18: Slice the pork into 5 mm strips and marinate 30 min in half the fish sauce, half the sugar, two crushed garlic cloves and the chopped spring onions.
Make the nuoc cham: dissolve the remaining sugar in 150 ml warm water, add the rest of the fish sauce, the lime juice, and the chopped garlic and chilli.
Taste and adjust: it should be sweet, salty and sour at once, with none dominating. This is the heart of the dish.
Grate the carrot into fine batons and steep 15 min in two spoonfuls of the nuoc cham.
Cook the noodles per the packet, rinse under cold water and let them drain completely.
Sear the pork 4 min a side in a very hot pan or under the grill, without crowding, until the edges caramelise.
Drop it still hot into a bowl of nuoc cham: it soaks up the sauce and flavours it in return.
Serve the noodles, the bowl of pork and sauce, and a platter of herbs and lettuce separately. Everyone builds their own.
q19: Make the marinade: gochujang, soy, brown sugar, grated garlic and ginger, sesame oil. It should form a thick paste.
Cut the chicken into 3 cm pieces and coat it generously. Leave 30 min, or overnight in the fridge.
Slice the sweet potato into 5 mm rounds: any thicker and it would not cook in the chicken's time.
Cut the cabbage into large 4 cm squares and the onion into wedges.
Heat a large pan over high heat and spread the sweet potato alone for 5 min, to give it a head start.
Add the marinated chicken and sear 5 min without stirring, so the marinade caramelises on the base.
Add the cabbage and onion, lower to medium, cover and cook 12 min. The vegetables release enough water that none needs adding.
Uncover, raise the heat 3 min and stir to reduce the sauce until it coats. Spring onions and rice on the side.
q20: Blend the spring onions, chillies, garlic, ginger, spices, thyme, soy, brown sugar, juice of two limes and the oil to a thick paste.
Score the skin of the thighs through to the flesh, three times each: the marinade penetrates instead of sitting on the surface.
Coat the chicken in the paste, pushing it into the cuts. Cover and refrigerate at least 4 h, ideally overnight.
Take the chicken out 30 min before cooking and heat the oven to 200 °C.
Lay the pieces skin up on a rack over a tray: the juices drip away instead of boiling the meat.
Roast 45 min, brushing with the remaining marinade twice during cooking.
Give it 5 min under the grill to blacken the edges slightly. Jerk is recognised by those almost-burnt marks.
Rest 10 min, squeeze over the last lime and serve with the rice.
f01: Slice the onions and melt them 15 min over low heat in two spoonfuls of oil, until translucent and sweet.
Spread them over the base of a gratin dish with the crushed garlic: this layer stops the vegetables above catching and flavours the whole dish.
Slice the courgettes, aubergines, tomatoes and potatoes into 4 mm rounds, as evenly as you can.
Stand them upright in tight rows, alternating colours. Packed tight, they stay upright and cook evenly.
Season, scatter with herbs and pour over the rest of the oil generously.
Bake 50 min at 180 °C. The vegetables should lose a lot of water and sink by half.
Scatter with breadcrumbs and give it another 15 min to form a crust.
Rest 15 min. A tian is eaten warm, which is when it tastes of most.
f02: Soak the salt cod 24 h in cold water in the fridge, changing the water four times. Without this the dish is inedible.
Poach it 10 min in the milk let down with an equal amount of water, with the bay, never boiling.
Drain it and remove skin and bones, flaking by hand: fingers find what eyes miss.
Boil the potatoes 20 min in salted water and pass them through a ricer, never a blender, which would turn them elastic.
Warm the oil with the crushed garlic without colouring it, 3 min, to scent it.
Work the cod with a fork, adding the garlic oil in a thin stream, then the potato, then a little of the warm poaching milk.
Taste before salting: the cod often brings enough. Add the parsley and lemon.
Spread in a dish, scatter with breadcrumbs and grill 20 min at 200 °C.
f03: Dry the chicken thighs and salt them. Brown 10 min over high heat in a casserole, skin down first. Set aside.
Sweat the sliced onions 8 min in the rendered fat over medium heat.
Dust with flour and stir 2 min: it should turn faintly blond without burning.
Deglaze with white wine, scraping the base, then reduce by half, 4 min.
Add the tomatoes, crushed garlic and 200 ml stock, then return the chicken.
Cover and simmer 35 min over low heat, until the meat comes away from the bone easily.
Meanwhile fry the mushrooms 6 min over high heat, separately, so they colour instead of weeping into the sauce.
Add them 10 min before the end and uncover to reduce. Parsley to serve, with the rice.
f04: Blanch the belly pork 10 min in boiling water, then rinse: this removes excess salt and clears the broth.
Return it to a large pot with 2 litres of cold water, the studded onion, thyme and bay.
Bring gently to a simmer and skim carefully for 10 min. A broth that boils turns cloudy and never recovers.
Cook 45 min covered, at the barest bubble.
Add the carrots, turnips and leeks in large lengths and continue 20 min.
Add the quartered cabbage and the potatoes and cook 25 min more.
Add the sausages for the last 15 min only: any longer and they burst and grease the broth.
Serve the meats and vegetables in a deep dish, the broth in cups alongside, mustard on the table.
f05: Separate the green leaves from the stalks: they cook at completely different rates, which is the classic mistake with chard.
Cut the stalks into 4 cm lengths and boil them 12 min in lemony water, which stops them darkening.
Add the roughly chopped green for the last 3 min only.
Drain everything and squeeze the leaves by hand to drive out the water.
Make the béchamel: butter and flour roux for 2 min, then the hot milk in three additions, whisking. Cook 6 min, add nutmeg, crushed garlic and salt.
Fold the chard into the béchamel with half the gruyère.
Tip into a buttered dish and cover with the rest of the cheese and the breadcrumbs.
Bake 25 min at 190 °C until golden and bubbling at the edges.
f06: Heat a litre of stock and infuse the saffron in it from the start: it needs time to give up its colour.
Keep the stock at a simmer beside the pan throughout.
Sweat the chopped shallot 3 min in half the butter over low heat, without colour.
Add the rice and toast it 2 min, stirring: the grains should turn translucent at the edges.
Deglaze with white wine and let it evaporate completely, 2 min.
Add the saffron stock a ladle at a time, waiting for each to be absorbed. Allow 18 min, stirring often.
Taste: the grain must stay firm at the core. Cut the heat and let it settle 1 min.
Beat in the very cold butter and the parmesan vigorously, until the risotto spreads slowly across the plate.
f07: Drain and rinse the chickpeas, setting a third aside.
Warm the oil gently with the crushed garlic, rosemary and chilli for 3 min: you are scenting the oil, not colouring the garlic.
Remove the rosemary sprig, add the tomatoes and cook 5 min.
Add two thirds of the chickpeas and 600 ml stock, and simmer 15 min.
Blend this base with a stick blender to a thick cream: it takes the place of a sauce.
Return the reserved whole chickpeas and bring to a simmer.
Tip the pasta straight in and cook 11 min, stirring often and adding hot stock if it thickens too much.
Rest 5 min off the heat. Serve with a thread of raw oil and parmesan.
f08: Soak the crustless bread in the milk for 5 min, then squeeze it lightly. This panade is what keeps the meatballs tender.
Mix the meat, bread, egg, parmesan, chopped garlic and parsley by hand. Do not overwork it or the texture turns rubbery.
Shape walnut-sized balls with damp hands so they do not stick.
Brown them 6 min in a pan over medium heat, rolling them, without trying to cook them through.
In a casserole, sweat the sliced onion 6 min, pour in the passata and reduce 10 min.
Lay the meatballs in the sauce without stacking them, cover and simmer 25 min over low heat.
Do not stir with a spoon: shake the pan gently, or the meatballs break up.
Add the basil off the heat. Serve with the spaghetti and the rest of the parmesan.
f09: Fry the crushed garlic 1 min in the oil, add the passata and reduce 15 min over medium heat.
Salt the sauce and add torn basil at the end.
Cook the pasta 3 min less than the packet says: it finishes in the oven and will absorb more liquid.
Loosen the ricotta with a fork and two ladles of hot sauce, so it spreads without lumps.
Toss the drained pasta with the remaining sauce.
Build in a dish: a layer of pasta, spoonfuls of ricotta, diced mozzarella. Repeat.
Finish with parmesan over the whole surface.
Bake 25 min at 200 °C until golden. Rest 10 min before serving.
f10: Dice every vegetable to 1 cm. The even size is the signature of pisto, which is eaten with a spoon.
Melt the onions 10 min over low heat in the oil, without colouring them.
Add the peppers and continue 12 min: they must go completely soft.
Add the aubergine and cook 10 min, adding a thread of oil if the pan dries out.
Add the courgette for 8 min, then the garlic and paprika off the heat for 30 seconds.
Add the peeled diced tomatoes and simmer 15 min uncovered, until no free liquid remains.
Make wells, crack in the eggs, cover and cook 6 min.
Serve warm with bread. Pisto is better still the next day, cold or reheated.
f11: Chop the pork shoulder with a knife and mix it with the beef, the milk-soaked bread, the egg, garlic and parsley.
Shape 3 cm balls and roll them in the flour, tapping off the excess.
Brown them 6 min in oil over medium heat, in two batches, then set aside.
Sweat the finely sliced onions 10 min in the same pan.
Toast the almonds 3 min dry, then pound them with the remaining garlic and the saffron: this picada is the traditional thickener, in place of flour.
Deglaze the onions with white wine, let it evaporate 3 min, add 300 ml stock and the picada.
Return the meatballs, cover and simmer 25 min over low heat, shaking the pan now and then.
The sauce should coat. Adjust the salt and serve with bread or potatoes.
f12: Cut the lamb into 4 cm cubes and dry them thoroughly.
Sear them in two batches in an ovenproof casserole, 5 min each, to a brown crust. Set aside.
Sweat the sliced onions 8 min, add the garlic and cinnamon for 1 min.
Pour in the tomatoes and 400 ml stock, return the meat, cover and bake 1 h at 180 °C.
Take the pot out, add the raw orzo and 600 ml of scalding stock. The liquid must cover generously, as orzo drinks enormously.
Stir once, then return to the oven uncovered for 25 min.
Check halfway and add hot stock if the surface dries: a youvetsi should stay creamy, not dry.
Crumble the feta over and rest 10 min before serving.
f13: Cut all the vegetables into 1 cm rounds or pieces. Unlike a tian, a briam is tossed: evenness matters less than volume.
Put them in a large dish with the crushed garlic, oregano, parsley, plenty of salt and all the oil.
Mix at length with your hands so every piece is coated. The oil is an ingredient here, not a seasoning.
Spread in a thick layer and add 150 ml water to the base of the dish.
Cover with baking paper and bake 45 min at 190 °C.
Remove the paper, fold gently and continue 30 min uncovered.
The vegetables should have shrunk a great deal and the edges caramelised. Add a splash of water if they dry out.
Let it cool 20 min before serving. A briam is never eaten scalding.
f14: Rinse the rice and soak it 30 min in cold water, then drain.
Poach the chicken 30 min with an onion and the spices in 1.2 litres of water, then lift it out and strain the broth.
Fry the aubergine slices and the cauliflower florets until coloured, 6 min a batch, and drain.
In a heavy casserole, line the base with onion rounds, then the boned chicken, then the fried vegetables in tight layers.
Tip the drained rice over without mixing and level it with a spoon.
Add hot broth to 2 cm above the rice. Maqluba means upside down: that is the whole point.
Cover and cook 35 min on the lowest heat, then rest 15 min off the heat without opening.
Put a large plate over the pot and flip decisively. Toasted almonds on top, yoghurt on the side.
f15: Sweat the finely sliced onions and celery 10 min in the oil.
Add the cinnamon and turmeric and stir 1 min off the heat.
Pour in the tomatoes and reduce 10 min, until the mixture darkens.
Add the rinsed lentils and 1.5 litres of water, bring to a simmer and cook 30 min.
Add the drained chickpeas and half the chopped herbs, and continue 10 min.
Slacken the flour in 200 ml cold water, without lumps. This tedouira is what binds a harira and gives it its velvety texture.
Pour it in slowly, stirring constantly, then cook 10 min over low heat to remove the raw flour taste.
Finish with lemon juice and the rest of the herbs. Harira thickens as it cools: let it down with water when reheating.
f16: Rub the chicken with oil, sumac, cumin and salt, and leave 30 min at room temperature.
Slice the onions very finely: they are half the dish, not a garnish.
Melt them 25 min over low heat in half the oil, until completely collapsed and golden.
Off the heat, stir in two good spoonfuls of sumac: they should turn purple.
Roast the chicken 35 min at 200 °C, skin up, until crisp.
Toast the pine nuts 3 min in a little oil, watching them: they burn in seconds.
Lay the pitta on a tray, spoon over the chicken cooking juices and give them 5 min in the oven.
Build: the bread, a thick layer of sumac onions, the chicken, the pine nuts. Lemon and yoghurt on the side.
f17: Cut the potatoes into 2 cm cubes and part-boil them 8 min in salted water, then drain and let them dry.
Blanch the spinach 1 min, refresh in cold water to fix the colour, then squeeze hard and chop.
Heat the oil and fry the potato cubes 8 min until golden on all sides.
Set them aside, then melt the sliced onion 6 min in the same pan.
Add the grated garlic and ginger and cook 2 min until the raw smell goes.
Add the cumin, turmeric and chilli and stir 1 min in the hot oil.
Return the potatoes, add the spinach and 100 ml water, cover and cook 10 min over low heat.
Finish with garam masala and lemon juice off the heat. Serve with the rice.
f18: Heat the oil and fry the finely sliced onions 12 min: you need real brown colour.
Add the garlic and ginger paste and cook 2 min.
Add the cumin, turmeric and chilli and stir 1 min in the oil.
Add the mince and raise the heat. Spread it out and let it colour 3 min untouched before breaking it up.
Cook 10 min more, stirring: the water must evaporate completely and the meat begin to fry in its own fat.
Add the diced tomatoes and 150 ml water and simmer 10 min covered.
Add the peas for the last 5 min, straight from frozen, as they cook very fast.
Off the heat, add the garam masala and coriander. Serve with the rice.
f19: Cut the pork into long strips 5 cm thick: this shape gives the most caramelised surface.
Mix the soy, half the honey, brown sugar, five spice, grated garlic and ginger, and the vinegar.
Marinate the pork at least 4 h, ideally overnight, turning once.
Heat the oven to 200 °C. Lay the strips on a rack over a tray holding a little water: the steam stops the marinade burning.
Roast 25 min, then turn and continue 20 min.
Reduce the remaining marinade 5 min in a pan with the rest of the honey, until it coats.
Brush the pork with this glaze and give it 5 min under the grill, watching: the edges should blacken slightly without burning.
Rest 10 min before slicing thinly. Serve with the rice and stir-fried cabbage.
f20: Start the rice; it will be ready at the same time as everything else.
Pound the garlic and chillies to a rough paste in a mortar. Chopped with a knife they would not give up as much scent.
Chop the chicken with a knife into small irregular pieces rather than slicing it.
Mix the soy, fish sauce and sugar in a bowl, so you are not measuring mid-cook.
Heat the oil very hot, throw in the garlic and chilli paste for 20 seconds, until fragrant.
Add the chicken and let it colour 2 min without stirring, then break it up and cook 3 min more.
Pour in the sauce, let it bubble 30 seconds, cut the heat and throw in all the basil at once: it should wilt without cooking.
Fry the eggs separately in very hot oil, frilled edges and running yolk, and set them on the rice.
f21: Cook the rice and leave it covered to rest.
Flatten the pork to 1 cm, nick the fat around the edge so it does not curl, and salt it.
Coat: flour, one beaten egg, panko pressed on firmly. Rest 10 min.
Fry 4 min a side at 170 °C, drain on a rack and rest 5 min, then cut into 2 cm strips.
In a small pan combine 120 ml water, the stock, soy, mirin and sugar. Bring to a simmer.
Add the sliced onion and cook 4 min until translucent.
Lay the breaded strips on top, then pour over the three remaining eggs, beaten very roughly, in a spiral.
Cover and cook 1 min 30: the eggs should stay loose. Slide onto the rice, spring onions on top.
f22: Use properly sour, aged kimchi. A young one gives a flat broth: it is the fermentation that makes the dish.
Slice the belly pork and render it 6 min over medium heat in a casserole.
Add the drained kimchi, keeping its juice, and stir-fry 5 min over high heat: this step concentrates its flavour.
Add the crushed garlic, the gochujang and the sugar and stir 1 min.
Pour in the kimchi juice and 700 ml water, bring to the boil then drop to a simmer.
Simmer 20 min uncovered, until the broth turns deep red and the pork is yielding.
Add the tofu in large cubes and the sliced onion and cook 5 min without stirring, so the tofu stays whole.
Finish with the soy, sesame oil and spring onions. Serve scalding with the rice.
f23: Poach the chicken 20 min in salted water with a halved onion, a garlic clove and the bay.
Lift it out and let it cool, then shred it by hand along the grain. Keep 200 ml of the broth.
Slice the two remaining onions and melt them 10 min over medium heat.
Add the garlic, paprika, chilli and oregano and stir 1 min off the heat.
Pour in the tomatoes and the reserved broth and simmer 15 min uncovered until the sauce thickens noticeably.
Blend the sauce with a stick blender to a smooth glossy texture.
Add the shredded chicken and simmer 10 min: it should soak it up completely and the sauce stop running.
Warm the tortillas and fill them. Cream, coriander and lime at the table.
f24: Cut the fish into large pieces and marinate 20 min in the juice of one lime, the crushed garlic, the paprika and salt.
Slice the onions and peppers into fine strips and cut the tomatoes into rounds.
In a wide casserole, layer half the onions, peppers and tomatoes.
Lay the drained fish on top without overlapping, then cover with the remaining vegetables.
Pour over the marinade and the oil, cover and cook 15 min over medium heat without ever stirring: shake the pot if needed.
Pour in the coconut milk and continue 10 min uncovered, at a simmer only. A hard boil would split the coconut.
The fish is done as soon as it flakes. Any longer and it disintegrates into the sauce.
Add the coriander and the second lime off the heat. Serve with the rice.
g01: Dry the chicken thighs and salt them. Damp skin does not colour, it blanches.
Brown them 10 min in the butter over medium-high heat, skin down first, without moving them until they release on their own. Set aside.
Wipe out the excess fat, keeping two spoonfuls, and sweat the chopped shallots 4 min without colour.
Add the sliced mushrooms and raise the heat: leave them 2 min untouched so they sear rather than weep, then 5 min stirring.
Dust with flour, stir 2 min, then deglaze with white wine, scraping the base.
Reduce by half, 4 min, then add 200 ml stock and return the chicken.
Cover and simmer 25 min over low heat, until the meat comes away from the bone.
Lift out the chicken, add the cream and reduce 5 min uncovered. Never boil once the cream is in. Parsley to serve, with the rice.
g02: Blanch the belly pork 15 min in boiling water and rinse it. Without this the whole dish is too salty.
Return it to a casserole with 2 litres of cold water, an onion studded with bay, the thyme and the garlic.
Bring gently to a simmer and skim for 10 min. Then cook 45 min covered, barely bubbling.
Rinse and pick over the lentils. Never soak them: they would burst.
Add them to the broth with the sliced carrots and leek, and the second sliced onion.
Cook 25 min without salting: salt toughens lentil skins until they are cooked.
Add the pricked sausages for the last 15 min only, or they would split and grease the dish.
Taste and salt now, cautiously. Slice the pork and serve on the lentils with the mustard.
g03: Put the meat in a large pot and cover it generously with cold water. A cold start lets the meat give its flavour to the broth.
Bring very slowly to a simmer, over 20 min. Rushing it clouds the broth beyond recovery.
Skim the grey foam patiently for 15 min, until the surface stays clear.
Add an onion halved and charred dry in a pan, which gives colour and depth, with the thyme, bay and peppercorns.
Cook 2 h at the barest tremble, never boiling, and not fully covered.
Add the carrots, turnips and celery, then 20 min later the tied leeks and the potatoes.
Continue 30 min: everything should be yielding without falling apart.
Serve the skimmed broth first, then the meat and vegetables with mustard, gherkins and coarse salt.
g04: Soften the crushed garlic 1 min in the oil over low heat, without burning it.
Pour in the passata, salt, add a pinch of sugar if it is sharp, and reduce 20 min over medium heat.
The sauce is ready when a spoon leaves a clean trail that closes slowly.
Drain the mozzarella and dice it, then leave it 10 min in a sieve: it releases a lot of water.
Cook the gnocchi in boiling salted water and lift them out the moment they rise, not a second later.
Toss them into the hot sauce with half the mozzarella and torn basil.
Tip into a dish and scatter with the rest of the mozzarella and all the parmesan.
Grill 12 min, until the top blisters and browns. Serve at once, scalding.
g05: Scrub the mussels and pull off the beards. Discard any that stay open after a tap on the worktop.
Rinse them several times in plenty of water, until it runs clear.
Open them 5 min over high heat in a large pan with the white wine and a lid, shaking once.
Lift them out as they open, shell three quarters and keep the rest in their shells for serving.
Strain the cooking liquid through a fine sieve or a cloth: there is always sand, and it is far too good to throw away.
Soften the sliced garlic and the chilli 2 min in the oil, add the halved cherry tomatoes and crush them for 3 min.
Pour in the strained liquid and reduce 4 min.
Cook the pasta a minute under, finish it 1 min in the pan with the mussels and parsley. Never salt before tasting.
g06: Brown the belly pork in large pieces 8 min over medium heat in a casserole, with no added fat.
Add the whole chorizo and sausages and colour them 5 min, pricking them so they render.
Set the meats aside and discard two thirds of the rendered fat: a fabada is rich, not greasy.
Sweat the chopped onion and garlic 6 min, then add the paprika off the heat and stir 30 seconds.
Return the meats, add the drained beans, the bay, the saffron and water to come level.
Bring to a simmer then drop to the lowest heat. A fabada must never boil or the beans break up.
Simmer 50 min uncovered, shaking the pot occasionally and never stirring with a spoon.
If the sauce stays thin, crush a ladle of beans and stir it back in. Rest 15 min before serving.
g07: Cut the thighs in two at the joint, which speeds the cooking and multiplies the browned surfaces.
Dry them and salt them generously 15 min ahead.
Heat the oil in a large pan and soften the unpeeled garlic cloves 4 min, then set them aside.
In that scented oil, sear the chicken 12 min over medium-high heat, turning to brown every side.
Return the garlic, add the bay and deglaze with white wine, scraping up the sticky bits.
Cover and cook 15 min over low heat, long enough for the garlic to turn creamy inside its skin.
Uncover and reduce 5 min: the sauce should become short and glossy, not liquid.
Chopped parsley and chilli to serve, with fried potatoes. Squash the cloves onto bread.
g08: A stifado is known by its whole small onions, in equal weight to the meat. Peel them without cutting them.
To peel them easily, boil them 2 min then refresh under cold water: the skins slip off.
Cut the beef into 4 cm cubes, dry them and sear in two batches, 4 min each, in the hot oil.
Set the meat aside and brown the whole onions 8 min over medium heat, rolling them around the pot.
Add the garlic, tomato purée and cinnamon and stir 2 min to cook out the purée.
Deglaze with the vinegar and let the sharpness evaporate 2 min, then add the tomatoes and water halfway up.
Return the meat, cover and simmer 2 h on the lowest heat. Never stir with a spoon: shake the pot.
The sauce should be dark and syrupy and the onions whole but yielding. Serve with the rice.
g09: Make the chermoula: blend coriander, parsley, garlic, cumin, paprika, the juice of one lemon, oil and salt to a thick green paste.
Coat the fish cut into large pieces and marinate 30 min in the fridge.
Slice the potatoes into 5 mm rounds: any thicker and they would not cook in the fish's time.
Line a tagine or wide casserole with the potatoes in a single even layer.
Lay the tomato rounds and pepper strips on top and salt lightly.
Pour in 150 ml water and two spoonfuls of chermoula, cover and cook 25 min over low heat.
Sit the marinated fish on the vegetables, add the olives and slices of the second lemon.
Cover again and cook only 12 min. The fish is ready as soon as it flakes; beyond that it falls apart.
g10: Cut the chicken into even 3 cm cubes: evenness is what stops you having dry pieces beside raw ones.
Crush the garlic to a paste with a pinch of salt, which mellows it and spreads it better than chopping.
Mix the yoghurt, garlic, juice of one lemon, spices, tomato purée and oil.
The yoghurt is not there for flavour but for gentle acidity, which tenderises without bleaching the meat as lemon alone would.
Marinate the chicken at least 4 h, ideally overnight, covered in the fridge.
Thread onto skewers loosely, so the heat can move between the pieces.
Cook 12 min in a very hot pan or under the grill, turning a quarter turn every 3 min.
Rest 5 min. Serve in warm pitta with tomato, red onion and parsley, and the second lemon.
g11: Vindaloo comes from the Portuguese carne de vinha d'alhos, meat in wine and garlic: vinegar is its central ingredient, not chilli.
Blend the vinegar, garlic, ginger and all the dry spices to a smooth paste.
Cut the pork into 4 cm cubes and marinate it in that paste at least 4 h, ideally overnight.
Brown the finely sliced onions 15 min in the oil to a deep brown. This is the sweet base that balances the acid.
Drain the meat keeping the marinade, and sear it 6 min over high heat in two batches.
Return everything to the pot with the marinade, the brown sugar and 250 ml water.
Cover and simmer 1 h 15 on the lowest heat, stirring occasionally.
Uncover for 15 min to reduce: the sauce should coat and the oil bead on the surface. Serve with the rice.
g12: A korma is a mild, pale curry: you are chasing neither colour nor heat.
Sweat the finely sliced onions 15 min over low heat, covered, without letting them brown. This is the hard part of the dish.
Blend them with the garlic, ginger and a little water to a smooth paste.
Heat the oil, add the onion paste and cook it 8 min, stirring: it should thicken without colouring.
Add the spices and stir 1 min, then the cubed chicken and coat it for 3 min.
Turn the heat to its lowest and stir in the yoghurt a spoonful at a time, without stopping. Added at once or too hot, it would split.
Add the ground almonds and 200 ml water, cover and simmer 25 min on very low heat.
Stir in the cream off the heat and rest 5 min. Serve with the rice.
g13: Put the beef in the freezer for 15 min, then slice it very thinly across the grain.
Mix it with the cornflour, a spoonful of soy and one of water, and leave 15 min.
Make the sauce separately: the rest of the soy, the chilli paste, vinegar and sugar, well dissolved.
Top and tail the green beans and cut them into 5 cm lengths.
Fry them 5 min in fairly hot oil, without blanching them first: the skins should wrinkle and blister, which is the texture you want.
Set them aside, keep only two spoonfuls of oil in the wok and sear the beef 2 min without stirring at first.
Add the chopped garlic and ginger for 20 seconds, then return the beans.
Pour in the sauce, stirring it first, let it coat for 30 seconds and serve at once on the rice.
g14: Put the beef in the freezer for 20 min so you can slice it into 2 mm strips, almost translucent.
Grate the pear finely: its enzymes tenderise the meat, and it is the traditional bulgogi ingredient.
Mix the grated pear, soy, brown sugar, garlic and ginger paste, and sesame oil.
Marinate the beef at least 2 h, mixing by hand to separate the slices properly.
Heat a large pan or plate over very high heat, until it smokes.
Cook the meat in three batches, 2 min each. All at once it would release its water and boil in the marinade.
Add the sliced onion to the last batch and let it just soften.
Combine everything, scatter with sesame and spring onions. Serve with rice and lettuce leaves to wrap it in.
g15: The rice must be cold, cooked the day before and kept in the fridge. Fresh rice clumps and crushes.
Separate the grains by hand before you start.
Cut the chicken small and have everything within reach: the dish takes four minutes.
Heat the wok empty until it smokes, add the oil and sear the chicken 3 min without stirring at first.
Push it aside, crack the eggs into the clear space and scramble 30 seconds before combining.
Add the garlic and onion for 1 min, then the rice, pressing it with the spatula to break it up.
Stir-fry 3 min over high heat, then pour the fish sauce, soy and sugar down the scorching sides of the wok rather than onto the rice.
Add the diced tomato and spring onions off the heat. Serve with a lime wedge to squeeze over.
g16: The name means old clothes, for the shredded look of the meat. You need a cut with long fibres.
Put the meat in whole in a casserole with water to cover, an onion, the garlic and the bay.
Bring to a simmer, skim, then cook 1 h 30 covered on the lowest heat.
Lift out the meat, keep 400 ml of the broth, and let it cool before shredding by hand along the grain.
Sweat the second onion and the peppers in strips 12 min in the oil, until they collapse.
Add the cumin and paprika, stir 1 min off the heat, then deglaze with white wine and evaporate 3 min.
Pour in the tomatoes and the reserved broth, add the shredded meat and the olives.
Simmer 30 min uncovered: the sauce should reduce until it coats the fibres completely, with no free liquid. Serve with the rice.
e01: Heat the oven to 150 °C and boil water for the bain-marie.
Chop the chocolate with a knife rather than breaking it: small pieces melt evenly.
Heat the milk and cream to a simmer, pour them over the chocolate and wait 1 min without stirring.
Then stir from the centre in small widening circles, to a smooth glossy ganache.
Whisk the yolks and sugar separately, then pour the warm chocolate in slowly, whisking constantly.
Pass through a fine sieve to catch any strands of set egg.
Fill the ramekins and bake in the bain-marie 25 min, with water coming halfway up.
The creams should wobble at the centre when you shake the tray. Chill 3 h.
e02: Choose thin-skinned oranges that feel heavy: those are the juiciest.
Peel them to the flesh with a knife, standing the orange on a board and following its curve.
Remove all the white pith, which is bitter and would spoil the dish.
Slice into 5 mm rounds over a bowl, to catch the juice.
Layer them in a dish, dusting each layer with cinnamon and icing sugar.
Toast the almonds 3 min dry, watching them: they brown all at once.
Mix the honey into the caught juice and pour it over the oranges.
Chill 1 h, then scatter with almonds and mint as you serve.
e03: Peel the pears keeping the stalks and rub them with lemon at once so they do not brown.
Make a light syrup: 600 ml water, the sugar and the split vanilla, brought to a simmer.
Lay the pears in and set a disc of baking paper on top to keep them submerged.
Poach 20 min over low heat, until a blade passes through without resistance but they stay whole.
Drain them and let them cool upright in a deep dish.
Heat the cream to a simmer and pour it over the chopped chocolate, wait 1 min then stir smooth.
Coat the pears in scalding chocolate as you serve: the hot-cold contrast is the whole dessert.
e04: Choose firm apples that hold up in a pan, like Golden or Gala.
Peel them and cut into thick quarters, all the same size.
Melt the butter in a large pan over medium heat and wait for it to foam.
Add the apples in a single layer and leave them 4 min untouched: they must colour before being moved.
Turn them and continue 4 min, then sprinkle with brown sugar and a good pinch of salt.
Let it caramelise 4 min, shaking the pan rather than stirring so they do not break.
Pour in the cream off the heat: it deglazes the caramel into a sauce within seconds.
Add the cinnamon and serve at once, warm, alone or over cold fromage blanc.
e05: Soak the gelatine 10 min in a large bowl of very cold water.
Zest two lemons before juicing all four: you cannot zest a squeezed lemon.
Whisk the yolks, sugar and lemon juice in a pan, cold, then heat gently.
Stir constantly for 6 min until it coats the spoon. Never boil, or the eggs will curdle.
Off the heat, stir in the squeezed gelatine then the cold diced butter, and cool completely.
Whip the very cold cream to soft peaks: over-whipped it would turn grainy.
Beat in a third of the cream to slacken, then fold in the rest with a spatula.
Divide between glasses and chill 3 h. Fresh lemon zest as you serve.
e06: String the rhubarb by pulling the fibres from the base of each stalk: they would stay stringy otherwise.
Cut into 2 cm lengths and mix with the sugar in a pan.
Leave 20 min without cooking: the sugar draws the water out of the rhubarb so none needs adding.
Cook 10 min over low heat with the split vanilla pod, without stirring at first.
Rhubarb breaks down very fast: the moment it slumps, it is done.
Add the halved strawberries off the heat; the residual warmth is enough to soften them.
Add the lemon juice, which revives the pink that cooking dulls.
Cool completely. Keeps four days and is eaten with fromage blanc.
e07: Sift the flour into a bowl and make a well in the centre.
Crack the eggs in and start mixing from the centre with a whisk, drawing in the flour gradually.
This method avoids lumps: poured in all at once, the liquid makes them inevitable.
Add the milk in a stream, then the cooled melted butter, the sugar and the salt.
Rest the batter 1 h at room temperature: the flour hydrates and the crêpes turn supple instead of brittle.
Heat a pan over medium-high heat and grease it very lightly with kitchen paper.
Pour in a small ladleful, swirling the pan with a flick of the wrist, and cook 1 min until the edges lift.
Turn and give 30 seconds on the other side. The first crêpe is always a failure: it is what sets the pan.
e08: Take the butter out 45 min ahead: it should be soft enough to dent under a finger without being melted.
Work it with the icing sugar using a spatula until smooth, without trying to aerate it.
Shortbread must not be aerated: that is what separates it from a biscuit.
Add the egg, vanilla and salt, then the sifted flour all at once.
Mix only until the flour disappears, without kneading: gluten would make them hard.
Shape two logs 4 cm across, wrap in film and chill at least 1 h.
Slice into 8 mm rounds and space them on a tray, as they spread a little.
Bake 12 min at 170 °C: blond at the edges, still pale in the centre. They firm up as they cool.
e09: Make the beurre noisette: melt the butter over medium heat in a small pale pan, so you can see its colour.
It foams, then the milk solids fall to the base and brown. Take it off the moment it smells of hazelnut, at about 3 min.
Strain it and let it cool: this browned butter is what gives financiers all their flavour.
Mix the ground almonds, icing sugar and sifted flour in a bowl.
Add the egg whites unwhipped, just loosened with a fork, and mix to a smooth batter.
Fold in the warm browned butter in a stream, then chill the batter 1 h.
Fill buttered moulds three quarters full and scatter with flaked almonds.
Bake 13 min at 200 °C: the edges should be well browned and the centre stay soft.
e10: Choose a ripe pineapple: a central leaf should pull out without effort.
Peel it, digging out the black eyes with a knife tip in diagonal channels.
Leave it whole rather than slicing it: that way it keeps its juice and confits instead of drying.
Score it all over, 1 cm deep, so the syrup penetrates.
Make a caramel with the brown sugar and two spoonfuls of water, then add the butter and spices.
Deglaze with the rum off the heat, standing back if you flame it.
Sit the pineapple in a dish, coat it and roast 35 min at 180 °C, basting every 10 min.
It is ready when glossy and amber. Slice at the table and spoon over the juices and lime.
e11: Heat the oven to 100 °C. Very gentle cooking is what separates a crème brûlée from a baked custard.
Split the vanilla pod and scrape the seeds into the cream and milk, adding the pod.
Heat to a simmer, then cover and infuse 15 min off the heat.
Whisk the yolks and sugar without frothing them: bubbles would rise and spoil the smooth surface.
Pour the warm cream onto the yolks in a stream, stirring with a spoon, never a whisk.
Pass through a fine sieve, then skim any foam from the surface.
Fill the ramekins and bake 1 h at 100 °C: the custard should wobble as one, not ripple.
Chill 4 h, then dust with brown sugar and blowtorch just before serving.
e12: Separate the eggs. The custard uses the yolks, the islands the whites: nothing is wasted.
Heat the milk with the split vanilla and infuse 10 min off the heat.
Whisk the yolks with 100 g sugar until pale.
Pour the hot milk in whisking, return to low heat and stir with a spoon in figures of eight.
The custard is ready at 82 °C, when it coats the spoon and a finger drawn through leaves a clean line. One degree more and it splits.
Sieve it at once into a cold bowl to stop the cooking, then chill.
Whisk the whites to firm peaks with the remaining sugar, then poach 2 min in simmering milk, turning halfway.
Drain them on a cloth. Serve on the cold custard with caramel and toasted almonds.
e13: Line the tin with the pastry, prick the base and chill 20 min: cold pastry does not shrink.
Blind bake 20 min at 180 °C with paper and weights, then 8 min without, to dry the base.
Brush the still-hot base with a little beaten egg white: it waterproofs it and keeps it crisp.
Chop the chocolate with a knife into fine even pieces.
Bring the cream and honey to a simmer, then pour over the chocolate in three additions.
Wait 1 min doing nothing, then stir from the centre in small widening circles to a smooth ganache.
Stir in the cold diced butter and a pinch of salt off the heat, which gives the shine.
Pour onto the cooled base and set 3 h at room temperature, never in the fridge which would make it brittle.
e14: Slacken the yeast in the warm milk, never hot: above 40 °C it dies.
Beat the flour, eggs and yeasted milk 8 min in a mixer: the dough should turn elastic and leave the sides.
Beat in the soft butter in three additions, continuing until it disappears.
Prove 1 h at room temperature, until doubled in volume.
Knock it back with a spatula, half-fill the moulds and prove another 30 min.
Bake 25 min at 180 °C to a deep golden brown. The babas must be quite dry to absorb the syrup.
Make the syrup: 600 ml water, the sugar, orange zest and vanilla, simmered then cooled to warm.
Submerge the cooled babas in the warm syrup for 15 min, turning them, then douse with rum. Serve with whipped cream.
e15: Unroll the puff pastry and roll it tightly into a log, then slice into 12 rounds.
Lay each round flat in a muffin hole and press it out with a wet thumb, from the centre upwards.
This spiral technique is what gives the characteristic concentric layers.
Chill the tin while you make the custard.
Make a syrup with the sugar, 80 ml water, the lemon zest and cinnamon, taken to 100 °C then cooled.
Slacken the cornflour in a little cold milk, add the rest of the milk and the cream, and cook stirring until thick.
Off the heat, stir in the strained syrup then the yolks, and sieve.
Fill three quarters full and bake 15 min at 250 °C, as hot as your oven goes: the black blisters on top are what make a real pastel.
e16: Warm the honey with the milk over very low heat, never boiling: boiled honey loses its scent.
The mixture should stay liquid and pourable, around 40 °C.
